#915. Metascience should be a source of evidence, not a means of control

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Efforts to apply metascience to research funding must put evidence and scientists front and centre.Credit: Alamy

The European Research Council made headlines last month when the news broke that those applying for one of its core grants had only a 5% chance of success. Partly as a result of applicants using artificial intelligence, the ratio of submissions to grants at the European Union’s premier science funder is now so skewed as to be little more than a lottery. Some funders are already using lotteries to select grant recipients, viewing these as a fairer way to allocate funding.

More self-reflection in research can lead to better science

More self-reflection in research can lead to better science

This is not a coincidence. The idea of distributing certain types of grant randomly has been tested experimentally over a number of years. It’s one example of how the field of metascience — the study of the practice of science itself — is having a real-world impact.

Metascience is not new. The world’s oldest journal devoted to the study of science, Nauka Polska, based in Poland, was founded in 1918 and is still publishing. Nature frequently reports on metascience, invites researchers to share their opinions and publishes primary science in the field. A set of studies released in April, for example, investigated the reproducibility, replicability and robustness of research in the social and behavioural sciences1–4. Developments in research funding, research organization, communication and evaluation are all aspects of metascience.

Metascience is also used by governments to support policy and funding decisions. In the past few years, a number of governments have established and funded metascience research units, as detailed in Seize the Meta Moment, a review by an international group of researchers and policymakers that was published last week by the Research on Research Institute in London (see go.nature.com/4z7pdt1). The author list includes members of some of these government-funded metascience units.

Huge meta-research project puts claims in social-science papers to the test

Huge meta-research project puts claims in social-science papers to the test

In one sense, this is positive, an example of policymakers seeking solutions informed by research. But the review’s authors point out that political attention also introduces risks — namely that the discipline could be misused to serve government agendas or to justify decisions that are not supported by a consensus of the evidence. They acknowledge that metascience will, to some extent, always be political, but that this should be acknowledged. And they urge politicians to use metascience as a learning tool and a source of evidence, but not as a means of controlling researchers.

In the United States, the Office of Science and Technology Policy has tasked all federal science agencies with establishing metascience capabilities. This was outlined in a July report, Science: A New Golden Age, which criticized excessive bureaucracy and slowness in US science, and embraced the idea of accelerating grant-awarding processes (see go.nature.com/3uj6pf5). One concern is that the US administration could use metascience to push through major changes, such as funding cuts, support for higher-risk research or the adoption of AI, without engaging the broader scientific community.

I built the UK government’s metascience unit — here’s what countries need to know

I built the UK government’s metascience unit — here’s what countries need to know

The United States is not the only country where researchers are worried about potential metascience misuse; concerns have also been raised in the United Kingdom, the first country to establish a government metascience unit. Last year, the nation’s main public funder of social science, the Economic and Social Research Council, announced a commitment to promoting economic growth. This is part of a broader economic push by the nation’s main public funder, UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), in response to a government priority.

The extent to which publicly funded science contributes to growth and the mechanisms underlying it are well-studied questions in the social sciences, and there are a range of views both supporting and critiquing the UK government’s objectives. It’s important that funders such as UKRI do not align themselves with just one view, and that the metascience unit does not reduce measurement of grant recipients’ performance to a metric that is itself still a matter of debate in the research community.

Why science has a credibility problem — and how to address it

Why science has a credibility problem — and how to address it

Most of the world’s science funding agencies were established when research careers were accessible to relatively few people. There is now a much larger and more mobile pool of researchers due, in part, to the expansion of universities and the globalization of science. Funding agencies need to change how they work to adapt as the world changes. That includes addressing the problem of falling success rates resulting from the greater demand for grants.

By far the best way for policymakers to use metascience to inform funding decisions is for them to work with researchers to create and implement tools designed to measure quality and competitiveness, and — as in science itself — to learn from experimentation and experience.

#913. Manchester’s soulless content machine football clubs sum up post-imperial Britain | Barney Ronay

United and City dominate the news cycle with stories so strange and vast they threaten to consume the rest of the league

In Manchester this weekend it was possible to bookend your Thursday‑to‑Sunday entertainment with two cultural events. First up, a debut screening of the re‑released and uncensored Ken Russell film The Devils at Trafford Odeon. And three days later, three miles down the road, Manchester United versus Aston Villa at Old Trafford.

As expected, one of these events provided a visceral cinematic experience, a deeply disturbing two-hour public meditation on the meaning of faith, blood, fear, power, ritual and the fetishising of objects, climaxing in an orgiastic crowd scene of depraved but undeniably erotic abandon, all acted out on a set in a state of glorious and performative ruin. And the other one was a film with Oliver Reed in it.

By the final whistle that wild 4‑4 draw at Old Trafford felt like a fitting endpoint to the opening quarter of the Premier League season. As we head into a 12‑day international break it is customary at this point to take a set of readings, to anatomise the season to date, to offer up a state of the Premier League address.

Five games since the last time we did this, not a great deal has changed. Brighton have maintained their luminous insurgent energy. The headline chart-breakers are Tottenham, up from second‑bottom to 11th. The official Home Office Spurs In Crisis threat level has been downgraded from Definitely In Crisis to Probably In Crisis A Bit Later On. Roberto De Zerbi no longer looks like a doomed and haunted cartoon caterpillar. Instead he looks like a feisty and fun haunted cartoon caterpillar.

Otherwise there has been only one story in town across that autumn segment. And that story is Manchester, and the extraordinary contortions of two contrasting, but deeply conjoined mega-clubs.

Manchester City’s run from October to November kicked off with the guilty verdict on almost all of their financial charges, followed by an adrenal victory at Anfield, and finally a run of three problematic league defeats. United have basically fallen through the floor in the same period: played eight in all comps, won one, and a point off the bottom of the Premier League table.

At the same time both Manchester clubs have dominated the news cycle, inexhaustible content machines, and the source of football-adjacent stories so strange and so vast they threaten to surge up over the seawall and consume the rest of the league.

It is necessary at this point to talk about Michael Carrick and whether he has been sacked yet (current answer: no). It seems likely that this will happen in the current break, once the designated replacement has been lined up. Another Manchester United paradox: only here, in the realm of the mid-season panic-sacking do we suddenly feel ourselves in the hands of a slick and well-practised machine. Stand aside. We’re old hands at this. Leave it to the experts.

But Carrick is of course essentially another bystander to the ongoing reactor core meltdown. He didn’t appoint Michael Carrick. He has done nothing surprising in his role as head coach, simply been the best Michael Carrick he can be, which is a Michael Carrick unqualified for this level of management.

Even the club executives captured by the TV pictures in insinuating close-up every week are essentially bit-part players, useful idiots for the regime: the director of football, Jason Wilcox, who looks every week a bit more like an office clerk trapped inside a hijacked foreign embassy trying to signal desperately with his eyes that he’s close to the edge and can someone in a flak jacket please appear at the fire escape window pretty soon. And the chief executive, Omar Berrada, who personally oversaw the Manchester City commercial sponsorship regime, and surely can’t be allowed to stay in his role at a listed company if the appeal against City’s charges is dismissed.

These are just the visible symptoms, not the cause. This is what happens when you run an institution where it is necessary to appoint people at significant levels who are willing to exist at a compromised level, who feel delighted to have the chance to run this organisation, even badly.

And by now it feels too easy to say the obvious thing. Manchester United have one competent but entirely self-motivated majority owner, for whom this has been a wonderful financial opportunity; and another owner whose only addition to the spectacle is to demonstrate the non‑transferable skills of the average billionaire.

We know this now. United are trapped in a cycle of self‑consumption. It is an ingrained, self-cannibalising decline, like a depressed post‑industrialised city in miniature. All that remains is rust, people and unspent heritage.

But it has also created something extraordinary in the past few weeks. Right now the Old Trafford match‑day atmosphere feels entirely unlike anything else, not just in sport but any other human activity at which you care to point.

The periphery is now enshrined definitively as The Event. Here is a man in sodden navy woollen menswear haunted by strange noises, striding the touchline like King Lear on his way to a golfing weekend. Here is the United crowd clamped together inside a clanky and leaking stadium, gripped by macro‑forces, shouting at the tides of power, a drama of alienation taking place just beyond the white lights around the lip of the stand.

The currents of energy are so mixed and nuanced. Who is cheering what? Where exactly is the love, the fear, the rage directed at this moment? Like all the best human dramas it is both sweeping and bathetic, thousands of human souls in that same shared space, all focused on an abstract idea, the act of faith and memory they identify collectively as Manchester United, while in front of them Harry Maguire trots about like an ageing police horse and Diogo Dalot attempts to play football with his legs on the wrong way round.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

To the unconverted, football can seem like a distraction, a silly thing, the society of the spectacle with the society part aggressively deleted. But there is still something noble about howling into this physical space, about expressing dissent, protest, rage, which is the opposite of so many things that are unsatisfying about the wider world: fakery, remote emotion, remote experience.

Take a look at the world that surrounds the team on the pitch: asset-stripping owners, branding overload, a club that is entirely committed to monetising your emotions. To rage at this thing is not just rational and human but an appropriate act of resistance.

This is where the autumn 2026 version of Manchester City also enters the picture. On the pitch City were muddled and unusually open in midfield during the 3-1 defeat by an excellent Nottingham Forest on Saturday. But something has changed around the club in this period, expressed most powerfully in that travelling support.

The urge to defy the independent tribunal verdict, to lean into being “villains”, has been a little baffling from the outside. It is hard to understand how truth, freedom, sunlight, the little man kicking against the pricks is compatible with swallowing the party line of an autocratic propaganda project.

But the space is more complex than that, the tension less linear. The City fans in Cheetos shirts waving inflatable mnemonic bananas, raising their fists to the world, have also become strangely captivating, persuasive, unexpectedly likeable.

Because this is also at bottom a protest against a world that feels beyond your reach. Forget the accounting regulation stuff and it isn’t hard to find plenty that is cheerless in the Premier League model, in the complete prostration of elite football at the altar of money. Whatever its source, no matter how muddled the logic, there is a base‑level majesty in this spectacle of defiance and collectivism.

If it feels addictive, moreish, impossible to look away from, then maybe this is because something authentic is happening in a world of fakery and illusions. The Manchester clubs feel in their separate ways like a version of their own city’s modern form, of the way post‑post‑imperial Britain has tried to create energy from inward investment or stripping its parts, selling its soul for some glass and steel high-rises and a tramline. It is a process that also includes turning supporters of a football club into product, a piece of staging, the trees on an architects drawing.

There is no obvious solution to this, no way of reversing that process given the selling off of land, control, intellectual property, just as it can seem like there is no obvious practical route towards the soft, comforting, previously attainable things Andy Burnham conjures up in his speeches about the future.

But it is interesting to see football directly confronting this alienation, expressing, however incoherently, that the only sensible response is a refusal to be silent. The Premier League is in its own way a perfect reflection of the nation, with its ailing but wealthy boomer generation, its lightweight pop-up entities filling the vacant spaces in the high street.

The other key story of the autumn period is of course Arsenal, who are basically London in the form of a football club, economically functional, geographically privileged, ticking along under its carefully curated restrictions. Is this the story of the season from here? Even with 28 games still to play it is hard to see Arsenal’s five‑point lead as anything other than a steady progression towards another league title.

At the same time every metric, from social media spikes to estimated TV figures, suggests that the event of the weekend was by some distance a theatrical but essentially meaningless 4-4 draw in the rain on Sunday night. Drink it in. Raise a fist to the world. Manchester has been the capital of English football for so long. It remains, even in a state of football‑adjacent crisis, its most potent spectacle, still able to provide a sense of something real in a post-real world.

#912. Injuries, noise & scalps - Wrexham's season so far

Wrexham are competing in the Championship for the second consecutive season under Phil Parkinson

With 15 games of the Championship season gone, Wrexham have steadied the ship.

Phil Parkinson's side responded to a run of three defeats in four matches by claiming four points from their home double header with promotion-hopefuls Middlesbrough and Wolverhampton Wanderers.

It ensured they entered the final international window of 2026 in positive spirits.

As the club action takes a two-week break, BBC Sport Wales looks at the highs and lows of the Red Dragons' season to date.

So how does Wrexham's performance so far this term compare to the same stage last season?

Wrexham's performances in the draws with Cardiff City and Watford early on were encouraging.

They made light work of dispatching strugglers Preston North End and have earned highly-impressive wins against top sides including Millwall, Southampton and Middlesbrough.

Defensively, Wrexham's expected goals (xG) faced of 18.17 is the fourth-best in the division.

They have also made just one error leading to a goal, the joint-best return alongside four other teams in the Championship.

Up front, Kieffer Moore - who scored 13 times for the Red Dragons in all competitions last season - has netted five goals so far this term, in addition to claiming two assists.

The Wales international's return comes from an xG figure of just 3.23, meaning he has outperformed his xG by 1.77. He has also won 68 aerial duels, with only four players in the league managing more.

Others such as Jacques Ekomie, Issa Kabore, Ben Whiteman, Joe Worrall and Callum O'Hare have shown real glimpses of settling in after joining on permanent deals in the summer.

Amid the increasing noise surrounding the club's struggles earlier on, Parkinson yet again demonstrated an impressive ability to remain grounded and get his side back on track.

In terms of the league standings, Wrexham sit six points adrift of the Championship play-off places and eight clear of the relegation zone.

So there is plenty of reason for the Wrexham faithful to remain optimistic.

A shock departure and key results - inside Wrexham's seismic week

Wrexham owners' presence uplifting - Parkinson

Parkinson 'pleased' with point against Wolves

When it comes to the numbers, only five teams have a lower xG total than Wrexham's figure of 16.80, while only three sides have managed fewer than their 50 shots on target.

Wrexham's four through balls made is - alongside Lincoln City - the joint-lowest in the division.

Home defeats by Birmingham City and West Bromwich Albion were particularly underwhelming, while the 6-0 thrashing at West Ham United represented a real low point.

Following the 2-0 loss to Blackburn Rovers in October, former Wales international Nathan Blake suggested Wrexham were losing their "fear factor" and that they were in danger of becoming "ordinary".

The Red Dragons then produced a lacklustre display as they were beaten 1-0 by Sheffield United.

It promoted a strong response from Parkinson who said he and his players would not shy away from any criticism.

After the draw with Wolves, midfielder Lewis O'Brien said of the post-Blades debrief: "I think we had to look at ourselves, deep down. It was a tough couple of days."

On the back of the 1-1 draw with Wolves, which came three days after an impressive 2-0 win over Boro, Parkinson declared his side had needed a reboot following the defeat by the Blades.

"We've had a bit of a reset this week in terms of what the performances need to look like for our supporters and everybody at the club," said the manager.

"We know we've got the capabilities to win games, but like everybody, you can easily have a capability to lose a game and you've got to be right at it.

"There's no 80% scenario in this division, everybody's got to be at it, focused and ready, and we really were ready in these two games. We can take a lot of credit from that."

Injuries certainly have not helped the club's cause, while there have been several off-the-field issues too.

The Red Dragons have been fined twice fielding ineligible players.

Chief executive officer Michael Williamson departed last week, with Shaun Harvey taking over as acting CEO.

It has clearly impacted the club's efforts in the opening third of the season.

"You always have things going on in football clubs, it's never smooth running anywhere," Parkinson said after the Wolves draw.

"But I think this has been particularly disjointed, for various reasons."

Ben Sheaf, Max Cleworth and George Thomason have all returned to action in recent weeks following significant spells on the sidelines through injury.

Nathan Broadhead is also closing in on a return, although it remains to be seen when last season's top scorer Josh Windass, Callum O'Hare and Liberato Cacace will be available.

Discussing the November international window, Parkinson said: "It's a chance to get some work in the lads who need to work and build on what we've done this week."

Unfortunately, Sam Smith is set to miss the remainder of the season and will undergo surgery this week after sustaining a serious knee injury at Sheffield United.

It will likely prompt the Red Dragons to scour the transfer market for an additional frontman in January given that Bailey Cadamarteri is the only other option behind first choice striker Moore.

Davis Keillor-Dunn could also potentially be recalled from his season-long loan spell at League One side Sheffield Wednesday - where he has scored five times in 11 appearances.

But the outlook on the campaign overall has certainly improved in the past week.

Wrexham fans hope more progress can be made over the coming months.

#911. Diego Gómez hits another stunner as Brighton beat 10-man Brentford to go second

Who can stop Brighton’s ­ascension in English and European football? They are setting standards, ­practices ­leaving almost everybody else ­trailing in their wake. A ­second‑place position in the ­Premier League would once have read like a glitch in a ­Football ­Manager ­session. Not in November 2026, where they appear the only team capable of throwing down any sort of challenge to Arsenal.

Under low winter sun, Brentford, an opposition to which Brighton are often, if lazily, compared, were ­swatted aside. If Keith Andrews’s team, and their fans at the Amex ­Stadium, could level blame at a couple of ­refereeing decisions, they received little chance of rescuing anything. Brighton squeezed them, toyed with them.

If Pascal Gross, scorer of a perfectly hit penalty, attempted to dampen expectations of a title challenge, his manager, Fabian Hürzeler, allowed fans to dream. “They should always be excited, it’s our job to make them excited,” he said.

A successful return to the Amex Stadium following five Brighton away trips, more than 5,000 miles on the road including victories at ­Manchester City and Getafe over the past two outings. Brentford returned to a stadium where they have never won in the Premier League. Normal service was duly resumed, any Brighton negatives coming in a failure to add to their first-half goals.

An up-and-under straight from the kick-off was a rare Brentford foray into the Brighton box. Bart Verburggen catching it on the full prefaced an easy afternoon for the Brighton goalkeeper. There are many further dimensions to ­Hürzeler’s team. Last week Paul Scholes, an unlikely ­progressive, declared himself an admirer of a “level of ­coaching” he suggested is ­unsurpassed in ­English football. “The one thing that is non‑negotiable is to always put the team first,” Hürzeler said.

Diego Gómez’s opener was not as spectacular as the halfway-line goal of the season against Crystal Palace but a beauty nonetheless. Caressing the ball first with his left and then with his right, he laid up a thrash past Caoimhín Kelleher. Its trajectory was unerring, unstoppable. Hürzeler revealed: “Yesterday, he changed to shooting with [his] left foot … I couldn’t see him scoring with his left foot. I asked him after where this quality came from.”

The path to a commanding win opened up. Igor Thiago did not last many ­minutes beyond his failed attempt to lob ­Verburggen. Scuffling in midfield with Chema Andrés, his shove was first ruled a yellow by the referee, Michael Oliver. In stepped the video assistant referee, Stuart Attwell: “violent conduct” and “with force” was the verdict from Stockley Park.

Afterwards, Andrews was ­visibly unhappy: “We’ve lost two games and both when down to 10 men. So we need to analyse ourselves first. In both scenarios we can do better. In both scenarios the opposition player has been the one to provoke the situation.”

Infact, both Yehor Yarmolyuk and Vitaly Janelt were dismissed against Liverpool, and if Andrews rues such lapses of discipline he was more unhappy at the initial decision’s video-assisted overturn: “The game is in a state now of a place I don’t particularly like.”

Straying beyond the confines of his technical area in a manner likely to add him to Mikel Arteta’s “massive storage of images” of such breaches, Andrews asked his team to dig deep but Brighton’s dominance of possession became near-total.

Luka Vuskovic, ­serving ­previously as a deep-lying playmaker, won the penalty. Keane Lewis-Potter’s ­panicked response to a physical 18-yard box mismatch was to snatch at the ­Croatian’s shirt. Gross’s penalty was struck as truly as Gómez’s goal. “We need to be cuter,” Andrews said. “I take real pride in the way we defend set pieces and we need to do better because that wasn’t good.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Andrews’s half-time ­adjustments, bringing on Yarmolyuk and Nathan Collins, was an attempt to protect Brentford’s goal difference. Brighton continued to pile on pressure, their ­possession share reaching beyond 75%. A set piece became Brentford’s sole route back, though Mathias Jensen’s diagonal into ­Verbruggen’s hands would not have passed muster in rugby’s Nations Championship.

Ironic cheers from the away end came when Brentford won a corner, and then another – rare excitement at Brighton’s defenders being asked to do something other than build an attack. The visitors’ fighting spirit at least sustained, though threatened to spill over. When Kevin Schade shoved ­Vuskovic to the ground by the touchline, another red card was a possibility, only for Oliver and Attwell to rule a yellow as sufficient this time.

Brighton’s push for honours and further horizons will require more than spectacular goals. “You see the Premier League, the margins, you look at the results – we are not ­getting carried away yet,” Gross said. “Every game we have to suffer a lot.”

Hürzeler, like Andrews constantly straying beyond the confines of his technical area, does not countenance any let-ups. When Brighton meet the unstinting demands of their coach, so many are left in their wing mirrors.

#910. Kane and Bellingham air strong views in England World Cup review

Kane and Bellingham made their views clear at the review

England players are understood to have aired strong views about their World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in a team meeting.

As BBC Sport reported in September, the Football Association (FA) process included canvassing the opinions of the squad - and it has emerged that took place at a 'full and frank' meeting with head coach Thomas Tuchel at the start of the September international break.

BBC Sport has been told the squad feel that now they have been able to have their say, they can move on from their heartbreak in Atlanta on 15 July.

And this was demonstrated in the last international break when England, after a narrow defeat by Spain in the first game, went on to win the next three matches impressively.

Burn replaces injured Guehi in England squad

Is Palmer's England career over under Tuchel?

'A beautiful story' as Bellingham brothers called up

The ramifications of the Argentina defeat, or perhaps more pertinently, the circumstances, meant some of the squad held grievances, with those feelings lingering and even growing throughout the summer.

In particular there was unhappiness about how Tuchel told them to approach the closing stages of the game after Anthony Gordon had given them a 55th-minute advantage.

Enzo Fernandez struck an equaliser with five minutes left, before Lautaro Martinez headed in a stoppage-time winner.

As reported by BBC Sport at the time, a number of senior England players held misgivings at Tuchel's instructions for the closing stages of the Argentina loss, believing the approach was too negative and defensive.

Hindsight, of course, is 20/20. England appeared to retreat in the closing stages of the last-16 tie against Mexico earlier in the tournament - but successfully defended a 3-2 lead to reach the quarter-finals to trigger scenes of joy at the iconic Azteca Stadium.

Nevertheless, certain players felt let down by the team's apparent pragmatism during the closing stages of the loss to Argentina amid a sense that going for the South Americans' jugular would have provided greater success.

Inevitably, the game against Argentina emerged as a key theme at the squad discussion.

It is understood that Tuchel pointed to the quality of the opposition as a key factor on why they eventually succumbed to two late Argentina goals.

There is, of course, merit to that argument. Lionel Messi was in the opposition team after all.

That said, it was not an argument the players in the meeting were prepared to universally accept.

There is a strongly held view within the England squad that their team, man-for-man, was superior to Argentina, who had 38-year-old Nicolas Otamendi on the field for the closing 18 minutes of the game.

All players were afforded an opportunity to air their personal views during the meeting.

As you would expect, captain Harry Kane was strong and forthright with his views.

Jude Bellingham, too, is said to have been particularly candid in expressing his belief that this current crop of England players were more than capable of continuing to take the game to Argentina.

Bellingham's contribution to the meeting is said to have underlined his growing influence within the England squad, with many believing the Real Madrid midfielder will become the team's captain once Kane is no longer in the picture.

If the air needed to be cleared after the World Cup then it appears those honest discussions at the end of September did the trick.

Barring the 3-2 defeat by Spain at Wembley in their first Nations League fixture in September, England have bounced back from the loss to Argentina emphatically - scoring 12 goals without conceding in three fixtures against the Czech Republic and Croatia.

Similarly, the fluctuating relationship between Bellingham and Tuchel seems to have improved, too.

"It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course but we are in a good place," Tuchel said last week.

"I love to be his coach. He's a top player, a very influential player and I think it goes both ways."

We will get a clearer idea of how 'Tuchel 2.0' is progressing in the next few days when England host Croatia on Thursday and travel to Madrid to face world champions Spain on Sunday.

A 4.1-billion-year-old meteorite discovered in the Sahara Desert offers a rare glimpse into Mars' early history.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A rose-colored rock discovered in the Sahara Desert may hold some clues to Mars' ancient geological history.

The meteorite, named Teghaza 001 after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered in 2022, weighs roughly 1.8 pounds (800 grams) and formed more than 4.1 billion years ago. Blasted off Mars by an impact before eventually landing on Earth, it is one of the three oldest Martian meteorites ever found. The extraordinary age and unusual mineral composition of Teghaza 001 offer a rare glimpse into the formation of Mars' early crust and how volcanic materials may have been altered by water, according to a statement from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.

"It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique,” research leader Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California said in the statement. "One of the paper’s reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars."

Unlike many Martian meteorites, Teghaza 001 contains a distinctive combination of igneous minerals and textures that preserve evidence of its complex history. Its mineral composition resembles materials observed in Mars' southern highlands by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.

Although researchers can’t pinpoint exactly where the meteorite originated on Mars, they have identified 13 potential locations on the planet where it may have formed.

"This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before," team member Lee Saper, NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley, said. "It records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water."The meteorite was initially identified as Martian based on its oxygen isotopes. To determine its age, scientists then examined tiny zircon crystals embedded in the rock. Using a specialized rubidium-strontium dating technique, researchers analyzed individual mineral grains on its surface, preserving it for future analysis.

The results revealed that Teghaza 001 was altered by water around 4.1 billion years ago, suggesting the rock itself formed even earlier. The mineral and chemical evidence points to a dynamic water cycle on ancient Mars, when liquid water interacted with the planet's crust and potentially left traces of its atmosphere as it gradually lost water.

Scientists believe further analysis of Teghaza 001 could reveal more about how water shaped the Martian surface and influenced the planet's evolution. The study also marks the first time researchers have used rubidium-strontium dating to analyze an ancient Martian meteorite, opening the door for the technique to be applied to other samples in the future.

"We've only scratched the surface," Liu concluded.

Their findings were published on Thursday (Oct. 29) in the journal Science. A separate study examining the meteorite's water content was published on June 10 in the journal Science Advances, offering additional insight into early Mars.

Samantha Mathewson joined Space.com as an intern in the summer of 2016. She received a B.A. in Journalism and Environmental Science at the University of New Haven, in Connecticut. Previously, her work has been published in Nature World News. When not writing or reading about science, Samantha enjoys traveling to new places and taking photos! You can follow her on Twitter @Sam_Ashley13.

#908. Crystal Palace poised to sack Pierre Sage and target Frank after Liverpool defeat

Frenchman under pressure after four successive defeats

Former Spurs manager Frank emerging as main candidate

Crystal Palace are poised to sack Pierre Sage after Sunday’s defeat by Liverpool left them bottom of the Premier League for the first time since December 2017, with Thomas Frank emerging as the main candidate to succeed him.

The Frenchman, appointed in mid-June to replace Oliver Glasner, has been under mounting pressure since a 5-0 defeat by Brighton last month. There have been few signs of improvement as Palace have slumped to four successive league defeats.

Sage has guided Palace to only two wins from their 10 Premier League games this season and they have the league’s worst defensive record, with 24 goals conceded so far. Although there were promising moments during the 3-1 defeat by Liverpool at Selhurst Park on Sunday, their habit of conceding goals from set pieces has not been rectified and it is understood the patience of the club’s hierarchy has worn thin despite Sage only being at the helm for 16 matches.

He is expected to become the first Premier League manager to be sacked this season on Monday. Palace are already believed to have started the process of bringing in his replacement. Frank, who was dismissed by Tottenham in February, spoke to Palace in the summer and is said to be keen for a new challenge after a successful spell at Brentford.

The former Nottingham Forest manager Sean Dyche also has his backers at Palace and would be seen as a safe pair of hands given his vast experience in the Premier League. Vítor Pereira, another former Forest manager, could be an alternative.

Sage signed a three-year contract in south London after leaving Lens, where he won the Coupe de France and qualified for the Champions League in his final season. Palace have lost their two main central defenders this year, Marc Guéhi moving to Manchester City in January and Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea in the summer. Two loan players – Axel Disasi and the teenager Honest Ahanor – were signed as replacements. Palace did not land one of Sage’s top targets, Malick Fofana.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Sage denied after the Liverpool game that his dream job had turned into a “nightmare” but suggested that Palace’s squad needed investment in January. “We have to adjust some positions during the winter transfer window to give more solutions,” he said.

#907. Incident-by-incident: Was it a bad weekend for VAR?

Manchester United's last-gasp equaliser against Aston Villa survived a VAR review for a potential foul

Whisper it quietly, but the statistics say video assistant referee decisions have been pretty good in the Premier League so far this season.

The Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel, which looks at every contentious decision and votes whether it is right or wrong, reported just two VAR errors after eight rounds of matches.

At the same stage last season, there had been six mistakes.

Then came this weekend, during which almost every top-flight game had a controversial decision.

BBC Sport looks at most of these situations - there really were too many to do them all - and assesses the likelihood that the KMI Panel will add to the list of errors.

Man Utd grab a point in dramatic fashion late on against Aston Villa

Incident 1: Penalty awarded to Manchester United for a foul by Boubacar Kamara on Matheus Cunha in the 16th minute.

Verdict: The spot-kick was awarded because the Villa defender went through Cunha to win the ball. Replays clearly showed the first contact was on the Brazilian's foot.

What the KMI Panel might say: This will be a correct decision.

Incident 2: Possible foul by Senne Lammens on Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki before Patrick Dorgu's 96th-minute equaliser.

Verdict : There are similarities to a goal Arsenal scored at Old Trafford last season, when William Saliba leant into United goalkeeper Altay BayÄ±ndÄ±r.

Lammens was not looking at the ball, which increases the chances of a VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel might say: With the higher bar for an intervention in the Premier League, and minimal contact, it is unlikely to be a VAR error to not disallow the goal.

Why Arsenal should have been given a penalty against Hull

Incident: Kai Havertz was pulled down inside the area by Nobel Mendy. The VAR, Michael Oliver, sent referee Farai Hallam to the pitchside monitor for a penalty, but it was not given due to an offside offence by the Germany international.

Verdict: BBC Sport covered this incident in detail on Saturday. As the foul happened before any potential offside offence, the penalty should have been awarded.

What the KMI Panel might say: Even though it feels wrong to reward a player in an offside position with a penalty, the law says otherwise and this is likely to be a mistake.

Should Bogle have seen red for this challenge in the Leeds v Tottenham game?

Incident: Jayden Bogle fouled Mathys Tel, with referee John Brooks giving the free-kick but no sanction for the Leeds player. The VAR, Tony Harrington, opted not to send Brooks to the monitor for a red card.

Verdict: BBC Sport covered the merits of this incident on Saturday. It was a difficult call for the VAR, because Bogle caused the foul with his supporting rather than his challenging foot. Still, it was a very painful challenge and some believe it should have been a red card.

What the KMI Panel might say: Was it an unfortunate incident, or a tackle which endangered the opponent? This will depend upon which former players are on the KMI Panel for this week, because it has split opinion among ex-pros.

Frank Lampard post-match interview - Everton v Coventry

All three incidents were covered in more detail by BBC Sport on Friday.

Incident 1: Coventry's Caleb Yirenkyi appeared to have his hair pulled inside the area by James Tarkowski, but no penalty was awarded.

Verdict: While the interpretation on hair pulling was relaxed for this season, meaning this would not be a red card, there appeared to be a yank of the hair by the Everton defender.

What the KMI Panel might say: Incorrect decision, penalty kick.

Incident 2: Another penalty claim for Coventry as Everton's Vitalii Mykolenko clipped Taiwo Awoniyi on the edge of the box.

Verdict: Replays shows that the contact on Awoniyi was made just before the line.

What the KMI Panel might say: Correct decision, no penalty.

Incident 3: Thierno Barry put Everton in front in the 61st minute, but there was a VAR check for a potential handball.

Verdict: The VAR determined there was no conclusive evidence for a handball, yet there does appear to be a deviation and the goal probably should have been ruled out.

What the KMI Panel might say: As the VAR does not have the super-zoom - this takes a few minutes to calibrate and is not available instantly - no VAR intervention might be supported. This was the case with a goal scored by Crystal Palace against Nottingham Forest. It could be a split vote.

Igor Thiago will be suspended for three Premier League games after his VAR red card for violent conduct

Incident: Igor Thiago was sent off following a VAR review after he caught the head of Chema Andres with his forearm.

Verdict: The Brentford striker can consider himself unfortunate, as there is doubt that he truly intended to catch the Spaniard in the face.

What the KMI Panel might say: It may seem like a soft dismissal, but the VAR intervention is likely to be supported because the law does say that a strike to the head should be a red card, unless force is negligible.

'Yellow card for me' - Dublin on Thiago red card

Incident: Crystal Palace were awarded a penalty three minutes into stoppage time for a foul by Milos Kerkez on Dario Osorio.

Verdict: We saw a similar incident the 2024-25 season when Arsenal defender William Saliba headed Joao Pedro after the Brighton striker had won the ball. This was voted to be a correct penalty decision.

What the KMI Panel might say: This incident is not quite the same as Saliba on Pedro, and more of a 50-50 clash. It may be voted as an on-field error, but not to the threshold for VAR.

Incident: Cole Palmer went down on the edge of the area under a challenge from both Luke O'Nien and Jules Ahoka, and asked for a penalty. Referee Jarred Gillett did not give a foul.

Verdict: A foul is determined by the first contact on the attacker. That a player falls into the box with contact continuing would not make it a penalty. Only on holding offences is continuing contact relevant.

What the KMI Panel might say: There is no conclusive evidence that any initial foul contact happened inside the area, so no penalty is likely to be supported.

Incident: Newcastle thought they had taken the lead at Craven Cottage, only for the goal to be ruled out for a foul by Yoane Wissa on Timothy Castagne.

Verdict: Matthias Jaissle was perplexed in his post-match interview, yet he would surely be furious if a Fulham player held one of his defenders back to create on onside corridor for another attacker to score.

What the KMI Panel might say: This is likely to be voted as a correct decision.

BBC Sport estimates that there are two decisions which the KMI Panel is very likely to log as a VAR error: not awarding penalties to Arsenal and Coventry.

Two further calls, Barry's goal and the potential red card to Bogle, may be errors but will depend who is on the panel and where their subjective opinion lies.

The others on the list are likely to be correct.

So we are potentially looking at two to four errors, which is not a good weekend.

#905. NWSL playoffs scheduling snafu: Washington Spirit keep Audi Field; Gotham move to Icahn

Washington to play in Saturday noon broadcast window

Shift to Northwest Stadium was reportedly in play

Gotham move to Icahn amid ‘atrocious’ pitch conditions

The Washington Spirit will play their NWSL semi-final at Audi Field after the club reached a deal to avoid playing a playoff game at Northwest Stadium, home of the NFL’s Washington Commanders. Top-seeded Gotham FC, meanwhile, will play their game at the 5,000-seat Icahn Stadium on Randall’s Island in New York City because of poor pitch quality at Sports Illustrated Stadium, their usual home.

The Spirit will play their semi-final against the Utah Royals on 14 November (Saturday) at noon, while Gotham FC will host the Kansas City Current on Sunday at 3pm.

The NWSL has had to maneuver through significant venue-availability conflicts in the past few days, balancing two sought-after national television broadcast windows with issues at the stadiums of the semi-finalists with home field advantage. Many of the teams in the league are not the primary tenants or owners of their stadium, meaning they are not able to exert full control or say over scheduling or conditions.

Audi Field has been the Spirit’s full-time home since 2023, and it has hosted raucous crowds for the team’s playoff runs, including Sunday’s 4-1 win over the Portland Thorns to advance to the semi-final.

However, a Division III college football game between the Coast Guard Academy and the Merchant Marine Academy was scheduled to be played at Audi Field on Saturday afternoon, a national TV window that the league would not be willing or able to move.

ESPN reported earlier this week that the NWSL had been preparing scenarios that would see the Spirit play their playoff game on Saturday at Northwest Stadium, a 64,000-seat venue in Landover, Maryland, roughly 10 miles north-east of downtown Washington where the team have never played a game in their 14-year existence, in the event that both the Spirit and top-seeded Gotham advanced to the semi-finals.

The Spirit are not the primary tenants at Audi Field. The stadium is owned and operated by MLS team DC United. The Spirit would not confirm if the college football game has been moved to a different location or date. As of Monday afternoon, it was still listed for its original time of 1pm on Saturday on both schools’ websites.

The location of Gotham’s semi-final against Kansas City was announced Monday afternoon. Though Sports Illustrated Stadium was available for the Sunday slot, the primary cause for concern was the state of the pitch. It has taken much wear-and-tear after hosting soccer and rugby matches in recent weeks, and would have hosted the semi-final just one day after MLS’s New York Red Bulls, the stadium’s owners, play a friendly against Liga MX side Club América.

During Gotham’s 1-0 win over Seattle in their quarter-final on Sunday afternoon, the venue’s field was patchy and sandy, with many visible brown spots. Reign captain Jess Fishlock described the field as “atrocious”. Gotham coach Juan Carlos Amoros apologized for the conditions and said the club attempted to mitigate the circumstances without success.

“Let’s be real, there’s no way a playoff game should be played on that shit,” Reign head coach Laura Harvey told ESPN. “I just can’t believe they’ve allowed it. They knew it last week.”

The league reportedly fined Gotham $10,000 for the poor conditions in their regular-season finale game on 4 November.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

“We as a team worked extremely hard to earn a home playoff berth. What we got was a field that is not the standard this club, this league or our fans deserve,” Gotham captain Tierna Davidson said in the club’s news release about the game relocation.

Icahn Stadium mostly hosts track events and is not well-trafficked, but has a natural grass pitch funded by MLS club New York Cit FC in 2024. It has hosted Gotham games in the past, including a regular-season match in July. Its capacity, though, is just less than half of Gotham FC’s average attendance this season.

“This was an extremely difficult decision, and one we did not take lightly,” said Yael Averbuch West, the president of soccer operations for Gotham FC, said in a statement. “After thoughtful consultation with coach Juan Carlos Amorós, our team captains and our ownership, we felt it was important to prioritize a playing surface that appropriately allows our athletes to perform at their best.

We fully understand and appreciate the impact this has on our fans, and we are equally disappointed that we won’t have the opportunity to play in front of more of our supporters at our home stadium. Unfortunately, we were faced with a difficult situation, and at the end of the day, the game is played on the field.”

NASA will host a first-of-its-kind air show and aerospace expo on Florida's Space Coast this weekend.

The show, called Max Power, will take place Saturday and Sunday (Nov. 7 and Nov. 8) at and around NASA's Kennedy Space Center (KSC). That name should be familiar to "Simpsons" fans, by the way: Max Power is an alias that Homer uses in the 13th episode of the show's 10th season. (He got it off a hair dryer.)

There will be a lot to see at NASA's event, so you should consider dropping by if you're on the Space Coast this weekend. (Tickets are required; you can buy them here.) Here are a few of the highlights.

NASA will also hold a livestreamed press conference on Saturday at 5 p.m. EST (2200 GMT) about its moon base plans. It will feature Fox, García-Galán, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and Dayna Ise, the acting director of the Utility and Infrastructure Office for the Moon Base Program.

There will also be dramatic flyovers on both days of Max Power, some of them by Isaacman, who's an accomplished pilot as well as a private astronaut. (He funded and commanded SpaceX's Inspiration4 and Polaris Dawn missions, which flew to Earth orbit in September 2021 and September 2024, respectively.)

According to NASA's Max Power schedule, Isaacman will perform flyovers both Saturday and Sunday at 11:58 a.m (in an F-5 jet) and 1:31 p.m. (in a MiG-29).

There will also be a lot to see as you're wandering the grounds at the Max Power sites.

The event "will showcase the newest aircraft, autonomous vehicles, technologies, and more defining the future of air and space," agency officials wrote in a Max Power description. "NASA will display its quiet supersonic X-59 plane, and agency partners will showcase moon rovers, spacecraft and more."

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. #902. The public trusts scientists with AI — more than it does anyone else

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Elliot Yates is an intern on the Nature Careers and Supplements team.

Almost half of survey respondents across nine countries thought that scientists’ use of generative artificial intelligence would make society better. Credit: gorodenkoff/iStock via Getty

Scientists are perceived as the group of people most likely to have a positive impact on society through their use of generative artificial intelligence, finds a survey published by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism in Oxford, UK, on 29 October1.

The survey, of nearly 19,000 people across nine countries, found that 46% of respondents think that AI use by scientists will make society better.

People who use AI tools on a daily or weekly basis were also overwhelmingly found to trust more strongly in the positive impact of the technology across all sectors than were those who seldom or never use it.

AI scientists are changing research — institutions, funders and publishers must respond

AI scientists are changing research — institutions, funders and publishers must respond

In 2024 and 2025, the team surveyed six countries, selected to provide cross-national variety among high- and upper-middle-income countries with broadly comparable levels of digital-media use. They were Japan, Argentina, France, Denmark, the United States and the United Kingdom. In 2026, Australia, Finland and Norway were added. Information was collected from about 2,000 people from each country.

Among the questions survey participants were asked was how much better or worse they thought each of ten groups’ use of generative AI would make their life or society. These groups included the government, politicians and political parties and ordinary people.

Scientists ranked top in terms of public trust, closely followed by health-care professionals. By contrast, politicians and political parties were perceived as having the worst impact through their AI use (see ‘With great power’).

The results did not surprise Rasmus Kleis Nielsen, co-author of the report and a communication researcher at the University of Copenhagen: scientists and health-care professionals performed well in the team’s 2025 survey, too2. As part of that investigation, respondents were asked whether generative AI would improve or worsen their experience of interacting with various sectors. Then, scientists ranked second of 12, behind only search-engine companies.

This year, the team explored why certain groups were and were not trusted by assessing different sectors’ perceived ability, benevolence and integrity in their use of AI. “Much of the public believe that scientists are able to use generative AI well, are relatively benevolent in their use of it and have relatively high integrity,” says Nielsen.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03578-y

Simon, F., Nielsen, R. K. & Fletcher, R. Generative AI and News Report 2026 (Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, 2026).

#901. Managerial 'inconsistency' hurting Ghana - Hughton

Kim Bjorkegren (right) is in interim charge of Ghana after Carlos Queiroz left the Black Stars by mutual consent

As Ghana prepare for two make-or-break 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifiers with women's coach Kim Bjorkegren in temporary charge, former boss Chris Hughton has called for greater consistency in the Black Stars dugout.

The West Africans face Somalia in back-to-back fixtures over the next week, having lost their first two games in Group C against Ivory Coast and The Gambia last month.

Those defeats resulted in the departure of Carlos Queiroz, whose brief period in the hot seat was characterised by uncertainty.

The Portuguese's exit means Swede Bjorkegren, who has been in charge of the Black Queens since January 2025, has now been asked to lead the men's team against Somalia.

"When you have inconsistency in the amount of time when a manager is staying, it's never good," Hughton told BBC Sport Africa.

"You want that consistency in the players [and] the players want that consistency in what they see in the manager."

Queiroz, who had two spells as Sir Alex Ferguson's assistant at Manchester United, was initially appointed in April and led Ghana to the last 32 of the Fifa World Cup, holding England to a goalless draw in the group stage, before announcing his own departure shortly after the team were eliminated 1-0 by Colombia in the last 32.

However, the 73-year-old was reappointed in early September, with the Ghana Football Association (GFA) praising his "extensive international experience" gained during time in charge of South Africa, Egypt, Portugal, Iran, Colombia, Qatar and Oman.

But Queiroz's return lasted less than a month following a 2-0 defeat by the Ivorians in Bouake and a 4-2 humbling against the Gambians in front of home fans in Accra.

"What I saw in the World Cup is that they represented the country very well, particularly the England game," said Hughton.

"And although it was very much a defensive outfit, there were opportunities to score."

Hughton, however, admits that regular sackings can create an "attitude" within a squad, with players knowing that "if he (the coach) doesn't do well then he won't be there".

Ex-Brighton boss Hughton reveals cancer diagnosis

Ex-Brighton boss Hughton backs mental health drive

Ghana suffered group-stage exits at the 2021 and 2023 Afcons under Milovan Rajevac (left) and Chris Hughton (right) before failing to qualify for the 2025 edition under Otto Addo (right)

Hughton's Ghana reign was also short lived.

Appointed as technical director by the GFA in February 2022, he moved into the head coach role in February 2023 but lasted less than 12 months before being sacked in January 2024 after his team failed to get out of their group at the 2023 Afcon in Ivory Coast.

The former Ireland full-back, who won two FA Cups and a Uefa Cup with Tottenham Hotspur and coached Newcastle, Norwich and Brighton in the Premier League, is one of five men who have taken on the Ghana job in the past six years.

Charles Akonnor, Milovan Rajevac, Otto Addo and Queiroz are the others, with the chopping and changing further illustrated by the fact that Addo had two spells in charge during that time.

Kwesi Appiah, the current Sudan boss, lasted 33 months during his second stint with the Black Stars between April 2017 and January 2020 - the longest anyone has managed since legendary Afcon-winning coach Fred Osam-Duodu in the late 1970s and early 80s.

With Ghana in real danger of missing out on a second successive Afcon finals, Hughton believes the situation has been exacerbated by under-investment and what he describes as "fearsome" competition across the continent.

"Many years ago Ghana were at a level that was, if not the best team in Africa, certainly right up there," said the 67-year-old.

"You've seen the emergence of so many other good African nations that have made the competition levels that much higher.

"Some of these countries have so many other problems, but I do think that there needs to be an injection of government money into the structure and into the system."

Hughton feels more needs to be done to encourage the development of the game in the West African nation.

"In Ghana, the local game that used to produce so many good players, the support level is not there," he said.

"They're playing on pitches that are not of a great level and the supporters are not coming.

"The supporters in Ghana love the Black Stars most, first and foremost, and of course the Premier League is massive there, but there isn't that support for the local game that there used to be.

"I think the government needs to do more as regards putting money into the infrastructure."

Coventry City midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi scored the only goal as Ghana beat Panama at the World Cup in June

While Ghana have failed to make it past the second round of Afcon since 2017, the country's World Cup record is far more impressive.

They have qualified for five of the past six finals since their debut in Germany in 2006, reaching the knockout stage on three occasions including a quarter-final appearance at the 2010 tournament in South Africa.

Having cruised through qualification for this year's World Cup in Canada, Mexico and the United States, losing only one of 10 games as they topped their group under Addo, Queiroz could reasonably claim he was hamstrung by multiple withdrawals ahead of his first Afcon qualifiers.

Six players named in the original squad, including Antoine Semenyo, Mohammed Kudus, Jordan Ayew and Baba Rahman, dropped out, followed subsequently by some of those called up as replacements.

Hughton hopes it is a situation which is not repeated - and which was not caused by the uncertainty around Queiroz's position.

"Whether that was a reason or not, I don't know. And I probably don't think so," he stated.

"You always want your best players and it's always a concern to the level of the group when you have so many players pull out.

"There isn't too much you can do about that [and] you have to work around that."

With the team's chances of reaching next year's Afcon in East Africa in serious peril, a lot rests of the shoulders of interim coach Bjorkegren.

As Ghana's long wait for a first continental title since 1982 continues, finding some long-term stability in the Black Stars' coaching set-up would be a good first step.

*Chris Hughton was speaking to BBC Sport Africa at the Best of Africa Awards

Khloe Kardashian gave fans a look at the "fairy tale-esque" Christmas lights that the Kardashians star decked out her home with: "Everything is so magical."

Khloe Kardashian is keeping up with the holiday spirit.

After all, the Kardashians star shared a glimpse into the "razzle and dazzle" from the thousands of Christmas lights adorning her Los Angeles home this season.

"I love the holidays for so many reasons, but when there are twinkle lights everywhere, it's amazing," Kardashian began in her Nov. 9 Instagram Story. "I love. And then these hedges are lined with lights. Everything is so magical."

All the trees and bushes along her curved driveway were decorated with bright lights leading to her home, which sat beside a decked-out massive oak tree with a swing. She praised, "It is like razzle and dazzle."

As for what lighting style the reality star—who shares kids True, 8, and Tatum, 4, with ex Tristan Thompson—went for?

"I love when my house is gingerbread style, so basically, you trim the perimeter of things," she explained, noting how bright the area was now. "It's so crazy what this does, how peaceful and fairy tale-esque and gorgeous these lights make this. It is absolutely spectacular, and I could not be any happier."

Though Kardashian has continued to prove that she's always doing the holidays amazing, sweetie, she credits Kris Jenner—mom to kids Khloe, Kourtney Kardashian, Kim Kardashian and Rob Kardashian Jr., with ex Robert Kardashian Sr., as well as Kendall Jenner and Kylie Jenner with ex Caitlyn Jenner—with their traditions.

"When I think of Christmas, you are the holidays, any holiday," she said to the matriarch on her Khloe in Wonder Land podcast in December 2025. “It could be like Presidents' Day. Every morning, that was a significant thing. You were like, 'Happy Presidents' Day!' There would be a napkin and something cute in our lunchbox."

The mom of two had followed suit when she got older, adding, "That's something that I definitely copy and paste from you. And I love it."

From decorations and desserts to presents and parties, Jenner had always prioritized celebrating the holidays.

"I remember all of our Christmas Eve parties, but not necessarily one over the other," Kardashian, 42, recalled. "It's just the tradition and the consistency of them that's so safe and nostalgic and comforting. I think it's so important that you've created those safe spaces for us."

#899. CF Montreal are for sale: What it means, how much it could cost, and what’s next for the MLS club

In an emotional press conference, CF Montreal’s founder and owner Joey Saputo refused to rule out relocation

In a rare press conference, CF Montreal owner Joey Saputo announced that his family was beginning the process of “initiating a structured sale process” of the MLS club. Saputo informed the public of his intentions on Monday afternoon, pausing multiple times to fight back tears after over three decades of owning the Quebecois club.

“This decision is neither driven by urgency, nor dictated by circumstance,” Saputo said in his initial scripted remarks. “It’s the result of a careful and deliberate reflection on where we stand today, and more importantly, on the opportunities that lie ahead for the club.”

Throughout his statement, Saputo stressed his desire to keep the club in Montreal, saying he hoped to find someone who “shares commitment to Montreal and who will ensure that the club remains in the city for many years to come.”

Yet, more than half an hour into the event after the floor was open for in-person questions, Saputo refused to rule out selling to a buyer who might move the club.

“I will not discount the club to the point of just giving it away just for the sake of giving it away,” Saputo said. “I want to be perfectly clear. I love this club. I will love this club to stay here. But if an owner comes in that doesn’t have the capacity to keep the club at the level that it needs to be at, and to spend the money that needs to be spent in order to bring in the players that this city wants to see, then at that point I’m not doing anyone a favor by selling it to someone just to keep it here.

“As much as I would love for this club to be here, if someone has the capacity to do it, and I feel that they have the capacity to do it, then I would love for this club to be here, and continue to build on what we did. But if there isn’t, and there’s an offer that comes in to relocate the club, and it’s in line with Major League Soccer and what they want to, then yeah, that’s where it’s going to be.”

Saputo declined to provide estimates for his selling point, nor for his and MLS’s timeline to find a suitable buyer. Saputo said the sales process will be conducted in coordination with MLS as well as the club’s retained investment bankers.

But based on recent history, Saputo stands to receive many times more than the $40m expansion fee he paid to join the league in 2012.

In January, the Illig family sold 71% of ownership of Sporting Kansas City to Peter Malouk at a $700m valuation. In May, the Haslem family sold a 37% stake in the Columbus Crew at a valuation of $900m. Both teams own their own home stadium; Forbes rated SKC as the league’s 16th most valuable franchise in 2025, while Columbus ranked 18th at the time of their partial sale.

As of June 2025, Forbes ranked CF Montréal as the second least-valuable club in MLS at an estimation of $435m, only ahead of Stan Kroenke’s Colorado Rapids. The club does own its own stadium, Stade Saputo – modestly sized at just over 19,000 capacity but on its day one of the better atmospheres in the league.

However, MLS’s decision to flip its season calendar means that Montreal could be in line to play more matches in the winter – a tough proposition in Stade Saputo’s outdoor environs. The Montreal Olympic Stadium, located next door, is due for a modernization and will reopen in 2028 but the club would be tenants there, should they move on a more permanent basis.

Saputo initially launched the club in late 1992, then as the Montreal Impact, serving as the club’s day-to-day steward for most of his ownership tenure. He guided the club through two decades in five different leagues before becoming an MLS expansion franchise, debuting in 2012. Two years later, Saputo led a consortium that bought a controlling interest in Italian Serie A side Bologna, where he remains president.

Saputo acknowledged an earlier aspiration, stated in early 2023, to position Montreal for long-term success on and off the field. That declaration came after the club had lost Wilfried Nancy to the Columbus Crew after two seasons of greatly outperforming expectations under the French manager. Nancy went on to win MLS Cup that season and reached the Concacaf Champions League final in 2024 with the Crew.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Meanwhile, Montreal have been at the very bottom of MLS since Nancy’s departure. Only three other teams have accrued as few points (139) over the past four seasons: DC United (139), Sporting KC (136), and Toronto FC (130). Montréal has won just one playoff game since 2016, with their best stretches directly coinciding with the brief tenures of striker Didier Drogba (from 2015 to 2016) and Nancy on the touchline (from 2021 to 2022).

Montreal have routinely been among MLS’s most thrifty operations this decade in terms of roster spending, both on salaries and transfer fees. Saputo acknowledged the need for the next owner to “start spending in line with some of the other teams,” a tacit admission of missing that mark.

“We’re going to continue to run the club,” Saputo said regarding the interim. “It will be challenging for us, but we are going to stay here until we find the buyer for the club.”

According to Saputo, yes. In opening that door, the club becomes the second of MLS’s three Canadian teams to be relocation candidates – the other being the Vancouver Whitecaps, who have been in the midst of their own sale and facilities quagmire.

These days, when an American sports league is looking to move a team, Las Vegas is an obvious first suitor. The city is no longer just for gambling and debauchery, with the NHL’s Vegas Golden Knights joining as an expansion side in 2017. The NFL’s Raiders became the first team to relocate to Nevada in 2020, leaving Oakland. The WNBA relocated the San Antonio Stars, now the Las Vegas Aces, in 2022.

Golden Knights owner Bill Foley initially looked into buying an MLS franchise to play in the city, only to ultimately buy AFC Bournemouth for £100m (roughly $121m at the time).

“MLS, unfortunately, requires a stadium to be built and, in the United States, that is costing $600-700m,” Foley said in 2022. “The franchise fee itself, I think, is $300m so you are into it for a billion dollars before you have a team. I thought Bournemouth was a bargain.”

Sacramento is another popular suggestion for relocation. The California capital was awarded an MLS expansion slot in 2019, but primary owner Ron Burkle put those plans on “indefinite hiatus” two years later citing financial strain due to the Covid-19 pandemic. MLS ultimately rescinded their claim as the ownership group folded, and awarded its 30th expansion slot to San Diego. The city’s second-division team, Sacramento Republic, is currently constructing a 20,000-seat venue to open in 2028 on the site which was previously intended to house Burkle’s MLS team.

Other cities that have confirmed interest in MLS, either at the government level or from local buyers, include Phoenix, Indianapolis, and Detroit.

Saputo’s stressing that local buyers won’t be given a discounted rate to keep the club in Quebec evokes memories of another longtime Montreal sporting organization. In the early 2000s, the MLB’s Montreal Expos struggled to find a buyer who could afford to keep the team in the city while meeting the requisite and rapidly growing financial might.

The Expos played their final season in 2004, relocating to the US capital and playing as the Washington Nationals for the ensuing 22 years to date.

A colossal coronal hole on the sun is unleashing a stream of high-speed solar wind that could spark impressive auroras Nov. 6-8.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The northern lights could put on an impressive display this weekend as a colossal coronal hole on the sun fires a stream of high-speed solar wind toward Earth. Minor (G1) geomagnetic storm conditions between Nov. 6 and Nov. 8, with a chance of moderate (G2) conditions on Nov. 7 and Nov. 8, according to NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC).

If G2 conditions materialize, the northern lights could be visible as far south as New York and Idaho.

The culprit behind the potential uptick in northern lights is a large coronal hole on the sun, a region where the sun's magnetic field opens up. They allow streams of charged particles known as the solar wind to escape more easily into space. Coronal holes appear darker in ultraviolet images because they are cooler and less dense than their surroundings.

And this particularly large — and rather oddly shaped — coronal hole is sending some seriously speedy wind our way.

The U.K. Met Office forecasts solar wind speeds between 342 and 404 miles (550-650 kilometers) per second, considerably faster than the typical speed of around 249 miles (400 km) per second.

The fast solar winds are expected to arrive around Nov. 6-7 and could persist through much of the weekend. It could interact with Earth's magnetic field, potentially triggering geomagnetic storms and fueling spectacular aurora shows. The stronger the storm, the farther south the northern lights can potentially be seen.

Under G1 conditions, auroras may be visible from northern Michigan and Maine, but if activity intensifies to G2 levels, skywatchers farther south, including those in New York and Idaho, could be in for a treat.

But remember! Aurora forecasts are notoriously tricky. Much depends on the strength and orientation of the magnetic field carried by the incoming solar wind, particularly whether it points southward, allowing more energy to transfer to Earth's magnetic field.

To give yourself the best chance of seeing the northern lights, keep an eye on those aurora forecasts, head somewhere dark away from city lights if you can, with a view of the northern horizon. To stay updated on space weather and know the best times and places to catch auroras, consider using a space weather app tailored to your location. One app I recommend is "My Aurora Forecast & Alerts," available on both iOS and Android. Another great tool is the "Space Weather Live" app on iOS and Android, which offers more in-depth insights into current space weather conditions and their potential for aurora activity.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

#897. Partick Thistle lose SWPL points for amateur player payments

Partick Thistle have dropped from eighth to ninth in the 10-team table

Partick Thistle have been deducted three points and fined Â£6,000 by the Scottish Women's Premier League for making payments to players who were registered as amateurs last season.

Thistle finished sixth last season and the points penalty means they slip one place to second bottom spot, three points behind Spartans, in the current 10-team table.

It follows a hearing on Monday at which the Glasgow club were found to be in breach of rules about making payments to amateur registered players and "submitting incorrect information regarding the submission of the certificate and undertaking document required as part of the membership criteria process".

Half of Thistle's fine is suspended until the end of season.

Thistle had the right of appeal but said on their website that the club "acknowledges and accepts the verdict".

They add: "The circumstances which led to the breach of SWPL player rule 37 and competition rule E31.11 were a result of a failure of internal process, which has since been addressed and resolved so that it can not occur in future.

"The club admitted the breach immediately when brought to our attention.

"We apologise to our fans for the mistake and its consequences."

Bottom side Aberdeen are now only four points behind Thistle.
