#896. Lecturer's bid to challenge Fifa president Infantino

Peter Auf der Heyde reveals his motives behind trying to run for the Fifa presidency

University lecturer Peter Auf der Heyde is launching an ambitious attempt to take on Gianni Infantino for the Fifa presidency.

The former journalist and football club owner is seeking to be nominated to challenge the incumbent Infantino - and wants to be paid a salary of just $1 (75p) per year if he wins the role.

South African Auf der Heyde lectures in journalism at Southampton Solent University and was previously sports editor of the Deutsche Presse-Agentur (dpa) in Germany.

He was president of the Grahamstown Soccer Association in South Africa and both owned and managed second-division side UDW FC in the early 1990s.

"I feel very strongly that there needs to be a challenge in any election," Auf der Heyde told BBC Radio Solent.

"There should not be an uncontested election and in this case Infantino needs to be challenged. It's important for accountability and transparency."

For Auf der Heyde to become a candidate to challenge Infantino in the March 2027 election, he will need to be nominated by five football associations.

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger is also considering standing against the current president, who faced calls to stand down following a controversial plan to sell off stakes in the governing body's competitions to private investors.

Infantino insisted he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football, and laughed off questions about whether he had considered resigning his position.

He is seeking a fourth and final term in the role but is also facing competition from Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association, and former Tottenham Hotspur and Switzerland defender Ramon Vega.

The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino is 18 November.

"I'm not asking for countries to vote for me, I'm asking for them to nominate me," added Auf der Heyde.

"Once you have a nomination and become an official candidate you can then ask questions [to other candidates] that you can't ask otherwise.

"Infantino earned around $6m (Â£4.49m) last year which I think is ridiculous. I would suggest that $450,000 (Â£337,259) is a very adequate salary and in my case I would ask to be paid $1 per year and after four years if I have maintained my promises then I can get the remaining money."

Wenger considers standing against Infantino

Auf der Heyde revealed that so far he has written to all 211 of Fifa's member associations, with replies already from the Jamaican and English Football Associations.

He broke down his manifesto for the role into three sections, with a key part of that being a new global competition for smaller footballing nations.

Only 48 nations qualify for the men's World Cup finals every four years with 163 missing out.

"I'd like to see an emerging nations World Cup," said Auf der Heyde, who covered 13 consecutive Africa Cup of Nations as a journalist.

"This would be for countries like Eswatini, Andorra and San Marino, who will quite frankly never qualify for the World Cup.

"They should be allowed in my view to play for a global competition where only these kind of countries have a chance to play.

"It would be wonderful if winning teams from that competition could then qualify further for the World Cup."

#891. Hera probe gets 1st good look at asteroid system clobbered by NASA's DART mission | Space photo of the day for Nov. 6, 2026

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Space.com's Sci-Fi Reader's Club. Read a sci-fi short story every month and join a virtual community of fellow science fiction fans!

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has gotten its first close-up look at the Didymos binary asteroid system. If that system sounds familiar, it's because it made headlines in September 2022 when NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) spacecraft smashed into it.

The aim of the DART mission was to test whether an impact could divert an asteroid away from a collision course with Earth. The purpose of Hera is to follow up on DART by making up-close observations of the Didymos system.

"The first thing we said was, 'Wow,'" Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel said in a statement about the image, which ESA released on Thursday (Nov. 5). "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART’s camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world."

The Didymos system consists of the eponymous 2,560-foot-wide (780 meters) space rock and its "moonlet" Dimorphos, which is about 530 feet (160 m) in diameter.

The DART mission impacted Dimorphos on Sept. 26, 2022, with the aim of causing a change in the orbital period of the moonlet. And it worked: Before the impact, Dimorphos completed one lap around Didymos in around 11 hours and 55 minutes. The DART collision reduced the length of this period by around 33 minutes.

The change is a result of the fact that Dimporphos is now traveling at around 2.7 millimeters per second more slowly than it did before the collision.

The newly released photo shows Didymos in detail. Just a sliver of Dimorphos is visible, below and slightly to the left of the main asteroid.

The changes caused by DART were small. But in a real Earth-threatening scenario, even such a tiny shift could help divert an asteroid on a collision course — as long as scientists get enough advance warning of its approach.

Hera's observations should help reveal what other changes have occurred on and around Didymos.

Scientists are already seeing that, while Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator as before the impact, many changes have occurred. This includes the creation of multiple boulders, craters, and patterns of grooves or ridges.

"Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 kilometer [0.62 miles] of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out," said Michael Kueppers, ESA’s Hera mission scientist. "We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."

Stay tuned to Space.com for more Hera findings from Didymos.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

#889. People don't know full story behind England exile - White

Ben White made his first England appearance in more than three years against Uruguay in March

Arsenal defender Ben White says people do not know the "full story" behind his decision to previously make himself unavailable for England selection - but says he would make the same decision again.

White, who has been named in Thomas Tuchel's squad for upcoming Nations League fixtures, left the Three Lions' camp at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar to return home for personal reasons.

He then made himself unavailable for selection for the rest of Gareth Southgate's reign, and was booed by some fans in March's 1-1 draw with Ukraine after returning to the squad under Tuchel.

Asked by BBC Radio 5 live's football correspondent John Murray what he would say to people who define his England career by what happened in Qatar, White said: "I think obviously people don't know the full story, because I [have] never said anything and I won't put anyone under the bus or share any of that.

"It's been amazing [though], obviously a bit tricky and not straightforward, but it is amazing to be here now."

White is now 29 and asked if he would have done anything differently in hindsight, he added: "No, I don't think I would.

"Obviously, I was a bit younger, I am a bit older now.

"I think as a person I am quite real and I think I made the decision that I would probably continue to make.

"So, one that I am not happy about, but obviously it happened and [it is] time to move on."

White came on for his first England appearance since 2022 in March's 1-1 draw with Uruguay and was booed by some supporters before he scored but also gave away the penalty that led to the visitors' equaliser.

After that, Chelsea midfielder Jordan Henderson said he and his fellow England players would always support White, while Tuchel said recently that the defender deserves "a new chapter" and "positive feedback from the crowd".

Asked how he dealt with the emotions of that night at Wembley, White added: "Before the game I was thinking 'don't not stand out, but [take it] nice and easy'.

"Then I came on and obviously got booed, then I scored, then I gave away a penalty.

"So, it was obviously full of emotions that night, [but] it was a good night."

England play Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, 12 November before taking on world champions Spain in Madrid three days later.

White is looking to add to his six England caps in this international break and said: "It is obviously an amazing privilege to be called up.

"The feeling is the same every time you do get this chance to play for England. It's one I am really looking forward to this week."

#888. Love Island’s Trinity Reveals Living Situation With Bryce in L.A.

Trinity Tatum exclusively told E! News at the 2026 EBONY Power 100 what her and Bryce Alakai’s life together in L.A. looks like after their Love Island USA win: “I make him come over all the time.”

Trinity Tatum and Bryce Alakai’s romance was never meant to stay in Fiji.

In fact, Tatum recently moved from her native Virginia to Los Angeles, where Alakai is based, following their win on Love Island USA season eight—and their new chapter is going swimmingly.

“I just got my apartment,” she exclusively told E! News in a joint interview with fellow islander Aniya Harvey at the 2026 EBONY Power 100 event on Nov. 9. “But it’s so funny because I literally just spent the night over Bryce’s house last night, so it’s like do a combination of I go over his house, he comes over mine.”

For them, having that balance in their relationship is crucial.

“He’s like, ‘I’m paying rent. I still have to go home,’” the 23-year-old quipped. “I make him come over all the time and he’s like, ‘Girl, I’m still paying rent to be here. L.A. rent is not cheap, honey.’”

That’s why Tatum and Alakai, 30, have “been mixing and dabbling” to get a "mix of both.” And the life they’ve built is exactly her type on paper.

“I’ve been in L.A. a lot,” she continued. “I’ve been around my man. I’ve been around all his friends and all of my girls.”

As for their holiday plans, the two will be making a splash with their loved ones.

“I am spending the holidays in Boston,” Tatum shared. “I want to spend a lot of it with my mom. We’re both spending it with both of our families.”

And Harvey is keen to do the same. After all, she revealed her plans to throw a huge holiday party in her native Atlanta, sharing she’ll be inviting “every single person.”

And that of course includes the rest of the core four ladies, including Kayda Bosse and Melanie Moreno, who Tatum shared she still talks to daily.

And Harvey, 24, makes it a point to stay connected as well. As she put it, “I feel like we do a good job of being in tune with one another.”

But in addition to finding both love and friendship in the Villa, the core four have also found success, a fact that Tatum shared they still “process” every day.

“I feel like every time we go to an event like this or anything we’ve been invited to, we are processing it,” she said. “Like, wow we’re really here.”

And Harvey echoed that sentiment, adding, “We take it in every single day. It’s such a blessing.”

"We showed that we can actually recover a planet that people previously couldn’t see."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sometimes science can seem really counter-intuitive. For example, occasionally in astronomy, you can see more with less light. Case in point: the emergence of a giant planet in observations made by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), when astronomers found a way to block out light from the planet's parent star.

The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet, in question is 51 Eridani b (51 ERI b), a gas giant with the same mass as around 11 Jupiters that orbits a star located around 97 light-years away. 51 ERI b was discovered back in 2015 by ground-based telescopes, but the planet was missing from observations of the system made by the JWST. That wasn't a failing of the JWST itself; no one is doubting the observing capabilities of the most powerful telescope humanity has ever hoisted into orbit around Earth. Instead, it was a result of starlight from the star 51 ERI A obscuring this intimidatingly massive world.

The brightest planets are 100,000 times fainter than their host stars, meaning spotting them is like observing a firefly hovering around a lighthouse. Even using a tool called a coronagraph to block the star isn't enough to reveal the planet, as that doesn't stop all the starlight.

The only solution to this glaring problem is a computer program to wipe out the starlight. "For the past 20 years, astronomers have tackled this problem by observing a different star and using its image as a reference," Jason Wang of Northwestern University explained in a statement. "Then, they subtract that reference image from the original observation to remove the unwanted glare to reveal faint planets that otherwise might be hidden."

There is a problem with this process, however. Even the most stable telescopes "wobble." For instance, the JWST requires cryocoolers to keep its NIRCam instrument super cold, and those coolers have little motors that can cause the mirrors to vibrate. This movement, however slight, causes a scatter in starlight. The result is enough glare remaining to obscure a planet, but Wang and colleagues developed a new approach to this problem.

The new approach taken by the team is dubbed Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP), and it involves creating a digital "twin" of a telescope. Essentially a virtual replica that simulates how starlight travels through the telescope's mirrors and reaches its detectors.

This twin is then fine-tuned to account for millions of tiny imperfections in the original telescope. The digital twin is then tweaked until it aligns with observations from the actual telescope. Astronomers can then remove the simulated glare from the original image.

To assess the validity of the technique, the researchers took a second look at JWST observations of two star systems with known exoplanets, HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani, and one system, TYC 5899, with no known planets.

The researchers found that, in terms of detecting faint exoplanets, FLIP outperformed conventional image-processing techniques two to 15 times. This led to ERI b emerging from data collected by the JWST two years ago.

"We showed that we can actually recover a planet that people previously couldn't see," Wang said. "This is real data in a real scenario. It was science left on the table because we didn’t have the right tools to analyze the data in the most optimal way."

The team hopes that FLIP can now be adopted by other astronomers in a bid to recover hitherto undiscovered exoplanets that have been hidden by the glare of their stars.

This could be a major boon for NASA's proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory, which aims to directly photograph Earth-like planets orbiting distant sun-like stars.

"We know of no planets around other stars that are like those in our own solar system," team leader Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez of Northwestern University said. "It's not that they don’t exist. It's that we cannot see them.

"Every time we improve our techniques, we discover new types of planets. By finding more planets, we can better understand how planetary systems form and evolve, and ultimately how typical our own solar system truly is."

The team's research was published on Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the journal Nature.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

#884. Savage denies media work is impacting role as manager

Peterborough are winless in their past six games in all competitions and were thrashed 5-0 at home by Reading in the FA Cup

Peterborough United boss Robbie Savage has rejected criticism of his work as a co-commentator and pundit as "a narrative that gets created if we're not winning games".

Savage was appointed on 2 October and won his first two games in charge but Posh have failed to win any of their past six games.

Before Saturday's 5-0 home defeat by Reading in the FA Cup, Savage co-commentated for TNT's coverage of AEK Athens v Real Madrid and Oxford City v Leicester City on Wednesday and Friday respectively.

The 52-year-old has also continued to present 606 on BBC Radio 5 Live, although did not feature on the post-match reaction show last weekend.

But Savage said his "commitment" to the League One club was absolute, telling the club's in-house media, external he was "first one in and last one to leave".

Since the 3-1 win at Leicester City on 10 October, Peterborough have drawn two and lost two of their next four league games to fall back to 22nd in the table.

They also missed out on a place in the quarter-finals of the EFL Cup after they were knocked out by fellow third-tier side Bradford City on 27 October.

Savage, who played as a midfielder for clubs including Derby County, Birmingham City, Leicester City and Blackburn Rovers, succeeded Luke Williams as Posh boss having previously managed Forest Green Rovers and Macclesfield.

"It's all about winning games of football," added Savage. "The narrative can be spun in any way but I'm a football man.

"It's my life. It's what I love doing and I love watching football. I'm not somebody who goes home and sits in front of the TV, or goes to the pub or has any hobbies outside of football.

"I'm not a golfer. I just love football. I'll go and watch every game that I can.

"I'm very fortunate that when I go and do games for TNT or 606, I'm getting knowledge all the time."

Savage added that he had also recently attended the games of local sides including Peterborough Sports and Wisbech Town.

"I put my hood up, I go to games, I pay to go in because I want to give back to grassroots football clubs," he said. "I go and watch every single game of football I can, I go and watch league games, because I love it.

"It hurts the fans the most when we lose, it hurts me a lot. But it's a narrative that gets created if we're not winning games of football.

"The bottom line is let's win games of football and then it all goes away."

#882. Mormon Wives' Jen Affleck Says She's "Not Doing the Best" Amid Divorce

Jen Affleck, who stars on Hulu’s upcoming Nov. 12 series Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, shared insight into her priorities amid her and Zac Affleck’s divorce.

Jen Affleck is swinging into a new chapter.

After filing for divorce from husband Zac Affleck, the Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County star shared insight into how she’s navigating her new normal.

“I'm not doing the best right now,” Jen—who is currently pregnant with her and Zac’s fourth baby—admitted to E! News in an exclusive interview. “I'm just taking one day at a time, and really just focusing on my kids. And obviously, the timing sucks, especially with me being pregnant.”

Nevertheless, she affirmed, “Ultimately, it was the best decision for us.”

And with that right decision bolstering her sails, Jen enjoyed sailing into the new horizon alongside her Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County costars Bobbi Althoff, Aspyn Ovard, Avery Woods, Madison Bontempo, McCall DaPron, Salomé Andrea, Ashleigh Pease and Jordan McClanahan.

For the Dancing With the Stars alum, the timing of filming Orange County made to an experience that was more freeing than her seasons on Secret Lives of Mormon Wives.

“What's funny is there was no reinventing this time,” the 27-year-old admitted. “I just showed up as me. I feel like for the past seven, eight years of my life, I've tried to mold myself into who I think people want to see, whether it be for my marriage or for TV or for the world. And this year was the first time that I really felt like I was reclaiming my identity and who I actually am.”

So, “going into the season, I just poured my heart into it,” she added. “Nothing was storyline; everything was real.”

That meant allowing the cameras to track her difficult chapter as it played out.

“I'm obviously not excited for people to see all the painful parts of the show,” she continued, “but I'm looking forward to people seeing the real, real me—and I guess I'm still trying to figure out who the real me is as well. So, we'll see that unfold in the future.”

As for how Jen showed up to The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, fans can tune in for the premiere on Thursday, November 12 on Hulu and Hulu on Disney+.

While Jen has in large part remained publicly silent on her divorce—though she did share two videos from her and Zac’s relationship, highlighting his less-than-ideal behavior—Zac shared a five-minute video sharing insight into their split.

“This is something we've been talking about for a long time,” he said of their breakup in the Nov. 5 TikTok. “Jen came to me about a year ago, after Dancing With the Stars, and told me she was unhappy and wanted a divorce. And I basically begged her to stay, told her I’d work on things, fix things, become whoever she needed me to be."

It was during this time that Jen became pregnant with their fourth baby, who will join siblings Nora, 5, Luca, 3, and Penelope, 16 months.

And, much like Jen, Zac wants to make sure their children remain his and her priority.

"That's really my priorities," he shared. "I feel like probably the thing that's eating me alive the most is I feel like I failed my kids, and I'm worried that I'm going to cause them damage. And I just hope that we can still give them a normal childhood, but as far as that goes, Jen and I are definitely on the same page of wanting to give them the best the best life we can."

As for why their marriage came to an end, he reflected, “Marriage is hard. Having your marriage in the public is hard. Raising kids is hard. And I think slowly over time we lost that spark."

Meanwhile, for a closer look at where Jen and Zac’s SLOMW: OC costars stand in their love lives, read on. And don’t miss the premiere of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County on Nov. 12.

Following her divorce from Cory Althoff, podcaster Bobbi Althoff is dating Tyler Hawkins, who plays a special role in Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County.

"He styles me, that’s how he supports me,” she told E! News in May, adding that the basketball player, "picks out my outfits every day. He styles me every day for the show. It’s great."

Aspyn Ovard, who filed for divorce from Parker Ferris in 2024 after eight years of marriage, is currently in a throuple relationship with married couple Billy Davis and Bri Davis.

After many ups and downs, Jen Affleck—who is pregnant with her and Zac Affleck's fourth baby—officially filed for divorce from her husband of seven years, E! News confirmed Nov. 4.

Despite ongoing relationship speculation, Salomé Andrea and Aaron Brimhall are still going strong as they prepare to welcome their third baby together. The duo, who married in 2012, also share 8-year-old twins Luca and Rue.

McCall DaPron—the sister of Mormon Wives' Mayci Neeley—shares four kids with husband Kirk DaPron, who she wed in 2011.

Ashleigh Pease and Nate Pease are rock solid after over a decade of marriage. "This 13th year together is one that has felt full circle!" she wrote on Instagram in September. "A season of fruits. Comfort. The happiest milestones."

Madison Bontempo and Kyler Steven Fisher, who wed in 2013, have been open about the highs and lows of their relationship. "Kyler and I aren’t perfect," she wrote on Instagram in October. "We’ve had arguments. We’ve had hard seasons. We’ve had moments we wish we could take back. And we’re not afraid to admit that."

But, she added, "Those moments aren’t our whole story. There’s also laughter, friendship, forgiveness, growth, five beautiful children, a million memories, and a love that has continued to evolve through every season of our lives."

Avery Woods and David Woods, parents to Ziggy and Stevie, are still feeling the love after a decade of marriage. As she simply put it, "my forever + always."

#881. PhDs worldwide are having a shake up — why now?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Jenna Ahart is a science journalist based in Washington DC.

Industrial PhD programmes are increasingly being utilized in fields such as public engineering.Credit: Emanuele Cremaschi/Getty

Yifan Wang didn’t realize that his thesis would be the first of its kind when he started his PhD, although he knew it was likely to be more applied than most. By the beginning of his project in electrical engineering and telecommunications at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, Wang had already established a connection with an industry partner to gather insights from network traffic patterns — such as how users stream videos.

But after Wang began his research, Australia rolled out its National Industry PhD Programme, in which students undertake research projects co-designed by universities and companies in return for a funding boost from the government and industry partners. The goal, according to the programme’s website, is to “create a flexible pipeline of researchers who can transition between academia and industry and have multiple career pathways open to them after completing their PhD”.

Wang joined the programme’s inaugural class in 2023 and spent the remaining three years of his degree not only with an eye towards practical applications, but also with a community of peers spread across Australia. And in May, he became the first student in the programme to submit his thesis.

Cake to the rescue: how these PhD students are cooking up a sense of community

Cake to the rescue: how these PhD students are cooking up a sense of community

“At the beginning of my PhD, I was a bit hesitant about whether I would want to do an engineering industry job or a research job,” Wang says. “But now, I’ve found my interest. I’m really determined to find a research position that solves real industry problems.”

As of June, the Australian programme has funded 448 awards and has received more than 1,000 applications during seven funding rounds. And it’s just one of many innovative PhD models. Governments in many other countries have launched programmes supporting industry-oriented PhDs.

“There’s certainly a lot of [experimental programmes] occurring around the world,” says Anthony Boccanfuso, chief executive of the University–Industry Demonstration Partnership, a non-profit organization in Columbia, South Carolina. The partnership leads the Industry-Integrated PhD (I-PhD) programme in the United States, which was launched in July. Although Boccanfuso says that conversations about re-evaluating the PhD model have existed for the past 15–20 years, there’s now a “sense of urgency because of this need for talent” in high-demand fields.

Intelligent manufacturing for rail transit systems is one of several areas to have benefited from China’s industrial PhD scheme.Credit: Xiao Benxiang/VCG/Getty

At the same time, researchers worry that the programmes might take away from fundamental research. When the I-PhD programme launched, chemistry Nobel laureate Carolyn Bertozzi wrote on the social-media website Bluesky that “most PhD students pursue industry jobs anyways — that has always been true. Use NSF funds to support basic science that industry won’t support”.

Boccanfuso’s organization will oversee more than 250 students with funding from the US National Science Foundation — which will make a US$47-million investment over the next five years — along with industry and university partners. Students are jointly mentored by university and industry advisers and are expected to spend at least one year completing on-site industry research. The programme aims to reduce the time taken to complete a PhD in the United States, from an average of 5.6 years to just 4 years. It will also prepare STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) students for industry careers, which is where most of them are going, Boccanfuso says. Although the initiative is only just beginning, it’s already received “overwhelming interest” from students and universities, he adds. Elsewhere in the world, including in China and the European Union, similar programmes have taken off.

As for why there’s been such a boom in these national-level initiatives, “it’s pretty straightforward”, says João Pereira, a civil engineer at the University of Minho in Guimarães, Portugal, who manages one EU-funded initiative. “It’s much easier to justify applied research than fundamental research because of the proximity to yielding results.” It can take decades for fundamental research to come to fruition, whereas applied research can deliver commercial applications — and therefore money and economic growth — “not immediately, but pretty close to it”, he adds.

Joshua Twiggs, who works in the medical technology industry in Sydney, Australia, and has supervised industry PhDs, says that these initiatives aim to harness a country’s already sophisticated education system as a driver of innovation. “How do we leverage the incredibly smart work happening in universities through to actual industry implementations?” Twiggs says.

Such programmes reflect “the growing recognition that knowledge is a key driver of economic competitiveness and innovation”, says Hans Parmar, a spokesperson from Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada in Ottawa, a government department focused on industry, commerce and scientific research. “Modern innovations are often too complex for a single individual, organization or even sector to develop alone,” Parmar adds. But these spanning initiatives mean that governments, universities and industries can all align their interests.

Julie Dubuit is a civil engineer at the University of Toulouse who took part in France’s Industrial Agreements for Training through Research PhD programme.Credit: Julie Dubuit

The trend can also be assigned to “the fact that academic positions in universities can only absorb a small fraction of PhD graduates”, says an official at the European Commission, the EU’s executive branch. That makes “industrial PhDs very attractive with regards to future employment”.

Meanwhile, China awarded its first batch of ‘practical PhDs’ in September last year. Rather than completing a conventional thesis, these students develop an innovative product, project or technique — such as intelligent manufacturing in rail transit systems. Since the law allowing these PhDs came into effect last year, more than 60 researchers have received practical PhDs.

“We encourage students to implement ideas that can meet real demand in society, rather than just coming up with concepts,” says Liu Chun, executive dean of the National College of Elite Engineers at Tongji University in Shanghai. Candidates’ success could be measured by “how many patents a student has, how many international or domestic industry standards they have participated in setting and whether their product has successfully passed a pilot test”, Chun says.

NSF rolls out ‘industry PhD’ programme — joining a global trend

NSF rolls out ‘industry PhD’ programme — joining a global trend

The European Union’s Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) programme offers applicants the opportunity to be part of industrial-doctorate networks of students, all of whom are focused on a single research topic. Each student has both an academic and a non-academic supervisor and must spend at least half of their fellowship on the premises of the non-academic partner. When all the cohort members and their supervisors come together, “it’s almost like a small conference”, says Pereira, who is part of a network that explores sustainable construction. “All these interactions force students to create a set of skills they won’t get anywhere else.”

One of the programme’s main goals, according to the European Commission official, is to “nourish the talent pipeline for boosting employability in industry”. A 2025 study found that two years after completing their fellowships, 66% of industrial doctorate graduates were working outside academia, compared with just 43% of graduates from the MSCA’s standard doctoral networks1.

#880. The fans at the foggy FA Cup game no-one could see

Ian Kirke struggled to watch his side's FA Cup first round match against Altrincham due to thick fog

For many football fans, an FA Cup win is the stuff of dreams. But for 690 Notts County supporters, thick fog meant they could barely see it happen.

Ian Kirke was among the Magpies fans whose view of Saturday's FA Cup first-round tie against Altrincham was obscured by fog, leaving many unable to see the League One side's penalty shootout victory.

The thick layer of fog provided chaos not just for the players and fans, but also commentators and camera operators at the J Davidson Stadium.

Kirke said fans had to rely on the cheers - or silence - from the home support during the shootout. "It's the most bonkers festival of football I've ever seen in my life," he added.

Heavy fog meant Notts County fans were unable to watch the penalty shootout that took place at the other end of the pitch

Lifelong fan Kirke, who lives in Berkshire, said the weather at kick-off was "like any normal match".

Before fog descended over Greater Manchester, Jacob Bedeau had given Notts County the lead just before the half-hour mark.

The hosts, who play in the National League, hit back as Lucas Weaver and Lewis Banks scored to give Altrincham a 2-1 lead.

With the conditions worsening, referee David Rock opted to continue with the tie, which saw the camera often unable to pick up the ball.

The referee's decision to continue the game paid off for Notts County, who levelled the tie at 2-2, when Callum Roberts scored from the edge of the box.

"It's like a fever dream" - commentators struggle through fog

"I can just about see the bright white numbers on their shirts, but I am struggling to see what is happening on the far side of the pitch," said BBC Radio Nottingham commentator Adam Hassell.

Former Notts County striker Mark Stallard was also commentating on BBC Radio Nottingham, and said: "We're looking around, and here in the press box no-one knows where the ball is! It's like a spot the ball competition.

"We genuinely cannot see the linesman or the players on the far side. It's slightly farcical having to commentate for radio listeners."

Lynda Lally said the fog got worse during the second half

Fellow Magpies fan Lynda Lally, from Beeston in Nottinghamshire, said the weather got "worse and worse" after half-time.

"For the other 45 minutes, we could only see what was happening once players emerged from the fog," she said.

The weather became "a cross between an eerie Christmas nativity gone horribly wrong - and the 1980s film called The Fog," Kirke said.

Kirke added the fog that led to an FA Cup third-round replay between Notts County and Wimbledon being abandoned in 2001 "wasn't as bad" as it was at Altrincham.

"I don't know what on earth had to happen for the referee to call it off," he said.

With the game going to penalties, Lally had hoped the shootout would take place in front of the Notts County fans so she could finally see the ball.

"Once we found out it wasn't, we were thinking what is going to happen because we can't see anything," she said.

"There was a deathly silence amongst the Notts fans when Altrincham fans at the other end were excited, and when they went silent, we went wild."

Kirke said his friend, who was struggling to see the action on TV, texted him updates during the penalty shootout.

"The only way we could ascertain what was going on was the reaction of the Altrincham fans," he said.

The sound of disappointment echoed around the stadium as Altrincham missed the target three times, before Rosaire Longelo slotted home the decisive penalty to seal a 3-2 shootout victory for Notts County.

"We heard the silence and we went into a massive roar knowing we had won," Lally added.

The Andromeda galaxy is one of the most distant things you can see with the naked eye. The difficult part isn't finding it. It's believing that faint smudge really is another galaxy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned.

I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way. Would she like to see it?

She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied.

There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened. We'd both seen photographs of M31 — a vast spiral galaxy with a brilliant center, sweeping dust lanes and hundreds of billions of stars. What we were actually looking at was a grayish blur that could easily have been mistaken for a mark on the eyepiece.

That apparent disappointment is now my favorite part of finding Andromeda because the unimpressive smudge is real. The light entering your eyes has been traveling across space for about 2.5 million years. No screen, photograph or telescope is necessary. You are intercepting ancient light in your backyard. Technically, the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), about 2.7 million light-years away, can be seen with the naked eye, so it is therefore the most distant object the naked eye can see. But not mine — I've never seen it. M31 is a much more realistic naked-eye target.

Early November is an excellent time to find M31 from the Northern Hemisphere. It's high and well placed during the evening, and this week the moon is becoming particularly cooperative. New Moon falls around Nov. 9, giving us several evenings with little or no moonlight to wash out faint deep-sky objects.

I usually begin with the star Alpheratz, one of the corner stars of the Great Square of Pegasus. You go two stars left, two stars up, and you arrive at M31. Another route — and a good way to check you're in the right place — starts in Cassiopeia, the distinctive W-shaped constellation high in the northeastern sky on autumn evenings. You can use its second V-shape as an arrow pointing straight at M31.

You can do that star-hop with the naked eye or a pair of binoculars, but M31 is visible to the naked eye only under a very dark sky. However, don't look for a miniature version of the photographs. Expect a faint, elongated patch with a slightly brighter middle.

There's another beginner trap to avoid. Images make Andromeda look compact, but its full apparent extent is enormous — several times the width of the full moon — and our eyes usually pick up only the much brighter central region. Once you know that, the smudge starts making more sense.

I'm going to look for Andromeda this week in the least heroic way possible. No expedition. No mountain-top observing location. No elaborate equipment. I'll wait until it is properly dark, step outside and then use Cassiopeia and the stars of Andromeda to work my way toward M31. I'll then reach for my 10x50 binoculars, which are rarely far from my side after dark, whether I'm at home or traveling. They gather enough light to make the galaxy's bright central region much more obvious without turning the exercise into a technical one.

A really useful skill here — whether looking unaided or through binoculars — is averted vision. Instead of staring directly at the galaxy, look slightly beside it. The more light-sensitive parts of the retina away from the center of our vision can make faint objects easier to detect. It feels slightly ridiculous the first time you do it — deliberately not looking at the thing you're trying to see — but it works.

If light pollution means you need binoculars, that still counts. No one gets a prize for detecting Andromeda unaided. After all, the extraordinary part isn't how you see it. It's what the light has done before reaching you. When those photons began their journey, modern humans did not exist. They crossed intergalactic space for roughly 2.5 million years and ended their trip in your retina. Stargazing is often described as looking back in time. With Andromeda, that phrase stops being a metaphor.

This is the week you've been waiting for if you want to spend time on faint objects rather than fighting moonlight. Without a bright moon overhead, spend some time on Andromeda, but revisit the Double Cluster in Perseus (NGC 869 and NGC 884). Binoculars show it beautifully, and unlike M31, it becomes more obviously crowded with stars as you increase magnification. Two other large, bright open star clusters in this region that look great in 10x50 binoculars are the glittering stars of NGC 752 in Andromeda and M34, a bright, hazy patch in Perseus.

Also keep an eye out for "shooting stars" because the Northern Taurid meteor shower peaks overnight on Nov. 11-12. Rates are low — around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions — so don't expect them to "light up the night sky". But they can produce bright, long-lasting 'fireballs' that can add a bit of pizzazz to a stargazing session.

Now that you've found its jewel, the Andromeda galaxy, it's worth trying to construct the constellation itself. As with M31, start with the Great Square of Pegasus and Alpheratz at its northeastern corner. Although it looks like part of the square, Alpheratz actually belongs to Andromeda. From Alpheratz, follow a curving line of stars away from the square through Mirach and on toward Almach. That gives you the basic shape of Andromeda — not the easiest constellation to imagine as a mythological princess, but a useful chain of stars to learn.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#877. How Nick Cannon Really Feels About Mariah Carey Prenup

Ten years after Nick Cannon and Mariah Carey finalized their divorce, the  America’s Got Talent alum, who was married to the singer from 2008 to 2016, revealed the details of their prenup.

Boy, if you wanna know whether Nick Cannon and Mariah Carey had a prenup—he’ll tell you.

Ten years after the former couple—who share 15-year-old twins Moroccan and Monroe—finalized their divorce, the former America’s Got Talent host confirmed they “absolutely” signed a prenuptial agreement before tying the knot in 2008.

“Mariah Carey, her entity, her global conglomerate, is gonna make sure she is protected,” Cannon explained during a Nov. 9 appearance on the On Par with Maury Povich podcast. “Had no problem with it whatsoever. And when it was all said and done, I think it protected both of us.”

Although their divorce wasn’t finalized for two years following their 2014 breakup, the 46-year-old—dad to 10 additional children with five different women—said the process felt “easy.”

Nevertheless, it’s not a process Cannon sees himself going through again, as he doesn’t see himself ever getting remarried.

“I think because of some of the natures of, like, unmarrying are not good,” he continued. “And it’s just the process—you don’t realize it takes so long and how draining it is.”

And while divorce “didn’t affect” his friendship with Carey, he saw how divorce creates pressure points in relationships.

“It really could have affected how we handled one another as friends,” he admitted. “I saw the traps of how this could have turned really bad if we didn’t step in and really engage as a family.”

For Cannon, he considered the friendliness that exists between he and Carey an exception when it comes to divorce.

“We handled it so well,” he added. “We handled it out of love. Never heard me say a bad thing about her. Never heard her say a bad thing about me. And we just kind of made it about the kids.”

Meanwhile, Cannon—who is currently in a non-monogamous relationship with Bre Tiesi and Abby De La Rosa—previously went so far to admit that he and Carey might have another shot at romance in the future.

“We belong together,” he quipped to E! News in 2024, going on to say that he would “be stupid” not to get back together with Carey.

As for why the fantasy hasn’t turned into reality? Cannon acknowledged, “She don’t want me.”

For more on Cannon’s family tree, keep reading…

Children No. 1 and 2: Moroccan Cannon and Monroe Cannon

Mariah Carey gave birth to her and Nick's twins on April 30, 2011. The two announced their split in 2015 after six years of marriage and finalized their divorce a year later.

Beauty queen Brittany Bell gave birth to her and Nick's first child together, a boy, on Feb. 21, 2017.

Brittany and Nick welcomed their second baby together, a girl, in December 2020.

DJ Abby De La Rosa gave birth to her and Nick's twin boys on June 14, 2021.

Model Alyssa Scott welcomed a baby boy with Nick on June 23, 2021.

However, just five months after the arrival of their son, Nick shared the devastating news that Zen had passed away from brain cancer. "Alyssa was just the strongest woman I have ever seen," he said on the Dec. 7 episode of The Nick Cannon Show. "Never had an argument, never was angry. She was emotional when she needed to be but was always the best mom and continues to be the best mom possible. So I've got to say thank you to my entire family but specifically to Alyssa."

"You never know what someone is going through," he added. "Hug your family. Kiss somebody. Tell them you love them."

Model Bre Tiesi welcomed her first child with Nick on June 28, 2022. The baby boy weighed 8 pounds and 10 ounces at birth.

"I did it. An all natural unmedicated home birth," Bre shared in a July 2022 Instagram post. "This was the most humbling / limit pushing yet awakening and completely empowering experience. I can't thank my team enough for delivering my son safely."

Nick and model LaNisha Cole welcomed a daughter on Sept. 14, 2022.

Brittany gave birth to her third child with Nick on Sept. 23, 2022.

Abby gave birth to a baby girl, her third child with Nick, in November 2022.

Alyssa gave birth to her and Nick's daughter on Dec. 14, 2022.

The model shared an Instagram video showing the Wild 'n Out star helping to deliver their baby. "Our lives are forever changed," she wrote. "Zen is in every breath I take. I know his spirit was with us in the room that morning. I know he is watching down on us. He shows me signs everyday. I will hold onto this memory forever."

She continued, "I will remember the sound of Nicks voice saying 'it's a girl' and the look of everything we've been through flash across his face. I will remember the sound of her crying out with her first breath and feeling her heartbeat against mine. My sweet girl, I got my surprise!! We love you Halo Marie Cannon!"

#876. Sisters in Sweat: how a former Spurs player got 20,000 Indian women into sport

A dinner-party question, a Sunday kickabout and an idea that snowballed. Nine years on, Tanvie Hans and Swetha Subbiah have taken sporting sisterhood to 10 cities

On a breezy evening in 2017, as conversations flowed and so did the drinks at a dinner party, Tanvie Hans was asked an all-too-familiar question at the table: “Hey, can you teach me how to play football?”

For the Indian-born British footballer, who played professionally in England, it was an easy yes.

After a little planning and some back-and-forth messages 17 women – mostly friends and acquaintances – turned up for Hans’ first football lesson on a Sunday morning in the southern Indian metropolis of Bengaluru, eager to discover the joy of the sport.

Nine years on from that impromptu football session, the group has grown into a community of 20,000 women across India. They may not be sisters by blood, but they are the Sisters in Sweat. Co-founded by Hans and the performance coach Swetha Subbiah, Sisters in Sweat is India’s largest women-first sports community, built to help women move more, play more and connect through a variety of sports.

From Chandigarh in the north to Chennai in the south, the initiative now spans 10 Indian cities, with football among its most popular offerings. “It wasn’t something that Swetha and I sat down to plan or even recognised was a gap in the market,” Hans, a former Tottenham and Fulham midfielder, tells Moving the Goalposts.

“But the moment we started these sessions they became successful and the community kept growing organically. That’s when we recognised that we were catering to an audience that is not being catered to in this way. And who better to do it than two women who are experts in the field?”

At Sisters in Sweat, coach-led football sessions are conducted two to three times a week, with participants free to choose between beginner and intermediate sessions, depending on their level of ability. The entry fee starts at about 300 Indian rupees – just under £2.50 – and women of all ages are welcome. You could be trying football for the first time, getting back to it or simply looking for a fun way to stay active.

The format is pretty simple, and the same one Hans and Subbiah used at their first gathering in 2017. The session begins with a quick huddle; everyone introduces themselves and the coach explains what to expect in the next 90 minutes. A warm-up follows before partner or group drills help break the ice within the group, which often features new faces every week. There is music playing in the background to create a celebratory mood and the session ends with a quick and easy 30-minute game of football.

A first-time participant often leaves with a smile, having ticked off a workout while meeting a bunch of strangers who they can now call friends. “You feel like, ‘Oh, I can actually play football and want to get better. I can’t wait to come back for the next session’,” Hans says. “Honestly, just being at the session opens doors for connection. It happens very naturally, and by the end of 90 minutes, you feel you belong here.”

Beyond nurturing new connections, Sisters in Sweat offers women something increasingly rare in India’s densely populated tier 1 cities: access to third spaces where they can show up and move their bodies without fear of judgment or safety concerns. With India’s fitness market projected to grow from $12.3bn (£9.2bn) in 2024 to $23.2bn by 2030 – an 88.6% increase over six years – Sisters in Sweat’s growth and expansion reflect the broader industry trend.

“My cousin, who is from the UK, was actively involved in our Sisters in Sweat sessions while she was in India on holiday. But after she returned to the UK, she wasn’t able to find a community like that,” Subbiah says. “I have heard the same thing from friends in Singapore and other countries. So, I think we, in many ways, have been the first movers to identify this.”

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

At the heart of Sisters in Sweat’s aim is to fill the gaping hole left by Indian women dropping out of sport, especially after school or college. In the country’s deeply patriarchal social structure, many women are often discouraged from venturing outdoors alone or playing sport recreationally. For many, having the freedom to stay out late at night is a distant dream or a luxury, at best.

“Once a woman leaves her role as a student, she moves on to her next role in life, which is typically becoming a wife,” Subbiah, who has been a Nike coach for over a decade, says. “Then she takes on all the household duties. Add a kid into the mix, and her personal time is minimised.

“There is also immense pressure on a lot of Indian women not to go out or play outdoors because they could catch a tan and look less appealing. A lot of the work we’ve done is to push past these social constructs and say, “Get a tan, it’s beautiful. Come out and play with us, you’ll feel great.”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Straight from its inspiring live performance at New York City's Carnegie Hall this past April, RadicalMedia's filmed presentation of the immersive living space documentary, "We Chose to Go to the Moon," is finally available for the rest of us to watch.

"We Chose to Go to the Moon" premieres Nov. 10 at 8:00 p.m. ET on PBS, PBS.org, and the PBS app, and we’ve got an exclusive clip to share featuring Mark and Kali Armstrong singing "Flight of Fancy."

With a poignant introduction by Oscar winning director Ron Howard ("Apollo 13"), "We Chose to Go to the Moon" recalls the extraordinary saga of the global space race and Apollo moon landings by actors portraying pivotal persons who made it all happen.

These roles include astronauts Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, Michael Collins and Ed White, Mission Control trailblazer Poppy Northcutt, "Hidden Figures" mathematician Katherine Johnson and members of the spacefaring families that remained on Earth, including Janet Armstrong and Betty Grissom.

This dynamic multimedia production is directed by Tony Award winner Michael Mayer ("Chess"), combining a unique fusion of theater, concert and documentary storytelling using rare archival footage alongside historic flags and artifacts taken to the Moon and returned home. It also revisits the ill-fated Apollo 13 mission and adds a special tribute to moonwalker Neil Armstrong performed by his son Mark and granddaughter Kali.

"We Chose to Go to the Moon" is created, written and narrated by historian John Monsky and stars Ian Weinberger ("Hamilton"), Skylar Astin ("Pitch Perfect"), Brent Comer ("The Outsiders"), Claybourne Elder ("Company"), Elizabeth Gillies (Netflix's "Dynasty"), Taylor Louderman ("Mean Girls") and Joy Woods ("Galileo"). Finally, Ian Weinberger ("Chess," "Hamilton") pulls it all together by conducting Broadway vocalists and the Orchestra of St. Luke’s in a selection of popular period music showcasing songs such as "Fly Me to the Moon," "Rocket Man," "Space Oddity" and "Sound of Silence."

We hope space fans around the world tune in to experience this sensational stage show that honors America's human spaceflight history!

#873. How Kelly Clarkson Helps Daughter River Navigate "Hard" Junior High

The Voice’s Kelly Clarkson shared insight into parenting her daughter River Rose, 12, as she navigates school, friendships and conflict during an exclusive E! News interview: "Junior high sucks."

Kelly Clarkson's daughter is spreading her wings and learning to fly above the drama.

As her and late ex-husband Brandon Blackstock's 12-year-old daughter River Rose experiences the ups and downs of junior high school, the Voice coach shared how she took a chance, made a change and guided the tween to break away from the woes of adolescence.

"I'm a pretty progressive parent, so I'm like, 'No, no. You're gonna make your own mistakes, and that's OK,'" Clarkson told E! News' Will Marfuggi in an exclusive interview on The Voice season 30 live show red carpet on Nov. 9. "I'm not like an 'I told you so,' but I do implement advice."

"They're growing up," she continued. "One's in junior high, and junior high sucks. It's a hard age with friends, and arguing and stuff like that. I do offer advice, and I've had my daughter come back and be like, 'So you were right.'"

But the 44-year-old—also mom to 10-year-old son Remington Alexander with Blackstock—will always help her daughter stand a little taller, even when she doesn't heed her mom's warnings.

As she explained, "I've had them be like, 'OK, so I didn't do that, and I should have.'"

While Clarkson is hitting all the right notes of motherhood, she's also had a pitch-perfect time on The Voice alongside fellow coaches Adam Levine, Queen Latifah and Riley Green.

Although the Maroon 5 frontman took home gold last season with Alexia Jayy, he couldn't wait another minute to focus on this season.

"He doesn't really brag like that," Clarkson said. "He's not that guy. I totally would. I'd be like, 'Good luck,' just for fun or whatever. But he's pretty chill about it."

But the "Breakaway" singer would be lyin' if she said she wasn't looking forward to working with Latifah and Green as the newest additions experience the live rounds for the first time.

"What's amazing about Queen is she's such a legend," Clarson emphasized. "I know people throw around the term legend a lot, but she actually is. She's done so much, be it Broadway and movie musicals, be it rapping, be it singing, be it acting, whatever it is. She's just always doing stuff."

Simply put, "That brought just a legendary kind of status to the show for us this season."

Meanwhile, the "Worst Way" singer has definitely brought more than wine and roses to the singing competition.

"Riley is just currently crushing it on the charts, like everywhere," she continued. "His career is blown up. It's a different point in his career for him, too. So it's fun. They're bringing that different energy of what's happening in their world at this chapter in their lives."

While fans wait to see who wins big during The Voice season 30, press the red button and keep reading for surprising secrets about the series.

Does the winner of The Voice get any money?

The winner of The Voice is promised a recording contract with Universal Music Group, the monetary value of which is technically unknown.

But while NBC and series producers have never confirmed any amount, the last singer standing at the end of the competition reportedly gets $100,000.

Past winners have acknowledged getting paid, season 18 champ Todd Tilghman telling People in 2020, "I don't have any immediate plans to make any drastic changes tomorrow. I don't know for sure the direction my life will go in. There's a possibility that that money might pay the bills for a little while."

But, he added, since his wife had promised their kids a trip to Disney World, he guessed he'd be splurging on that too.

Not that the value of the music opportunities that open up for the winners should be discounted.

“I’ve got a catalog of songs. I have a lot of writer friends I want to collaborate with," season 27 winner Adam David of Team Bublé told Parade in May 2025. "The plan is to put out some music and go on to work. We’re going to put out some music, and we’re going to hit the road."

How does an aspiring contestant get to The Voice's Blind Auditions?

In addition to individual recruiting (such as when producers reached out to Frenchie Davis eight years after she was on American Idol), The Voice traditionally held in-person auditions around the U.S. Lately, however, the talent search is online, judges holding virtual open calls and weeding through video submissions to find singers who then may get a chance to sing for the coaches in hopes that at least one of them turns around.

Contestants must be at least 13 years old when they embark on their audition journey. The hopefuls have 90 seconds to introduce themselves and sing. They can sing anything they want but, per the show's FAQ page, they're encouraged to pick a tune "that best suits your voice and represents you as an artist."

Judges listen to auditions for "five or six days with approximately 18 to 20 auditions per day," executive producer Audrey Morrissey told SheKnows in 2018. Once they're selected for the blind round, she explained, "Artists are with us for several days prior to [their audition] to rehearse with our band, work with wardrobe/styling and camera block on the audition stage."

Then there's the filming to put together the packages introducing some of the hopefuls and their families, all of which came as a surprise to season six alum Ddendyl Hoyt. "I had no idea that reality TV was filmed kind of like a drama," she told the Washington Post in 2014, “So everything is filmed in segments and that’s kind of the longest process of it all.”

How many times can you audition for The Voice?

If at first you don't make it out of the untelevised rounds—or onto a team if you do make it to the blind auditions—you're free to try out as many times as you want, albeit only once per season.

"I can't be a mean judge," coach Reba McEntire, who won season 25 with Asher HaVon, told Newsweek in 2023. "It's good just to say, 'If you want to come back again, try it again next season, maybe a song that suits you, one that you're really comfortable with and that really shows your talent,' give them advice and encourage them to come back."

As of season 28, there's also the Carson Callback card to be played, in which longtime host Carson Daly grants an aspiring artist who didn't get any takers another shot.

Do The Voice contestants get to pick out their own clothing?

The show has a massive wardrobe department that ensures the contestants take the stage in elevated fashion—once they've made it onto a team.

"We shop for each artist to come up with great looks," Morrissey told SheKnows. "Once we get to the live shows, looks are customized for each specific performance."

How much time do the coaches really spend working with The Voice artists?

The celebrity coaches might not be pulling all-nighters, but they're invested in getting their teams ready for the battle rounds and beyond.

"The coaching sessions take place over four days," Morrissey said, "and the actual battle performances take two days."

Meanwhile, she added, how involved a coach gets with each artist "depends on the coach. Some love a big production and like working out all the details…Other coaches mainly focus on the music and arrangement for the performance."

Some coaches "are avid texters while others email," Morrissey added. "All off-camera interactions intensify as the artists move through the competition and the stakes get higher."

But it takes a village, former contestant Hoyt telling the Post, "What they don't show is all the coaching that comes from the staff: The vocal coaches, the band director, the producers, everyone has notes for you."

Snoop Dogg told Access Hollywood in September 2025, "The behind-the-scenes people don't get the credit that they deserve. It's a lot of people, moving things, making it happen…All of these people back here that make our job easy, all we gotta do is walk onstage and do what we do."

Who picks the songs the contestants sing on The Voice?

Between coaches and artists, Morrissey said, “The No. 1 communication is about song choice.”

The artists can theoretically offer their two cents when it comes to picking their songs, but usually the coaches rule on that front.

Season one's Frenchie—who competed under O.G. coach Christina Aguilera's tutelage—told Cosmopolitan in 2021 it was "always hysterical when the judges say, 'I don’t think that was a good song choice for you,' and I'm thinking, you picked that song.”

On the flip side, season 24 winner Huntley credited coach Niall Horan with helping him find his way, telling NBC Insider the One Direction alum "knows how to pick songs, I'll tell you that."

What sort of resources are available to help The Voice artists tend to their mental health?

Aspiring contestants are screened beforehand to see if they seem emotionally ready for the pressure that lies ahead, and then the show employs mental health professionals to help the artists both during and at the end of their journey.

“We had to start visiting to check on our well-being," season six alum Kat Perkins told Cosmopolitan of the counselors on staff. "The minute you are eliminated, you walk from that stage and into the psychiatrist’s office for a debriefing. They make sure that you talk about it. It’s very needed because you’ll never go through anything like it again. It’s traumatic and you’re not really emotionally set up to do something that big that quickly."

How do the chairs on The Voice really work?

The coaches are masters of their own domains, the big red chairs evolving over the years but always boasting the ability to turn around at the push of a button. In 2018 they received a sleek upgrade, including the addition of three more buttons—giving each coach the chance to block a fellow coach, once per round, from getting a chance at claiming the contestant behind the voice.

Not unlike a luxury car seat, in addition to an automobile-caliber aluminum frame and shiny paint job, each chair has self-adjusting heaters ("Me and Reba, we're the butt-warming kings," Snoop quipped to Access Hollywood) and dual cupholders (as requested by former coach Blake Shelton).

But, according to Perkins, the dramatic whoosh sound the chairs make when they turn around is added in post-production.

"You almost don’t notice it," she told Cosmo, "especially when you’re focusing and singing to the crowd that’s in the studio."

While congenial ribbing between coaches is part of the show's DNA, it was unclear at times over the course of the 16 seasons they were on The Voice together if Blake and Adam Levine were as exasperated with each other as they seemed.

"We are constantly at each other's throats, and sometimes we really do get mad at each other," Blake told The Tennessean in 2017. "We're those two guys you knew in high school where we have this bond that is unexplainable. It brings out the best and worst in both of us. It truly is an explosive relationship. And I know every trick to get under his skin."

Translation: "He's one of the best friends that I have, but I still want to kill him sometimes."

And even though they haven't competed against each other since 2019, Adam knows what the fans want.

"The Voice season 1 after party, at my house with dips--t @blakeshelton," the O.G. coach captioned a throwback pic ahead of his return to the show in February 2025 for season 27.

Meanwhile, subsequent crops of coaches were far less likely to tweet out each other's private phone numbers.

"You spend so much time together," Niall said during an NBC sit-down, "and I was hoping it wasn't going to be like this TV relationship where the cameras go around and we're like [feigning enthusiasm], 'Hey, Snoop Dogg!' I was always nervous about that, doing the show in the first place. I just didn't want it to be like a forced relationship, and it hasn't been that at all."

#872. From W-M to the No 10, shirt numbers tell a story of football’s tactical evolution

In the days before squad numbers, the number on a shirt was an indicator of position, as well as the attributes a player was supposed to demonstrate

Ultimate 1-50: check out our complete list of players

Numbers have a fascination. The No 10 is revered almost everywhere, but perhaps most especially in Argentina, where it denotes the playmaker, the enganche, the quasi-mythical figure who links the front and back of the team. Liverpool and Manchester United have reasons to celebrate their No 7. Ajax retired No 14 for Johan Cruyff, Milan their No 3 and No 6 for Paolo Maldini and Franco Baresi respectively and Birmingham their 22 for Jude Bellingham as gestures of respect for their abilities. Other numbers have been retired to mark premature deaths: the No 20 at Liverpool for Diogo Jota, the No 23 at Manchester City for Marc-Vivian Foé, the 21 at Espanyol for Daniel Jarque.

But numbers are not just about individuals. In the days before squad numbers, the number on a shirt was an indicator of position, and the expectations of particular numbers in particular cultures, as well as the attributes a player in that shirt was supposed to demonstrate, themselves tell a story of tactical evolution.

The earliest evidence of teams wearing numbered shirts seems to be in a game between the Australian sides Sydney Leichhardt and HSM Powerful in 1911. The University of Chicago’s American football team wore squad numbers in 1913. There were experiments with numbers on sleeves in baseball from 1916. There were isolated efforts with numbered shirts in the American Soccer League, which began in 1923, and, especially, in the USA’s Challenge Cup. Various touring sides began to experiment with numbered shirts through the 1920s and, in August 1928, on the opening day of the English league season, two games featured numbers. Chelsea’s outfielders wore 2-11 in their Second Division game against Swansea, while Sheffield Wednesday wore 1-11 and Arsenal 12-22 in a First Division clash at Hillsborough.

Similarly, 1-22 numbering was used in the 1933 FA Cup final, in part because Everton and Manchester City were forced to wear change kits due to a colour clash, although the presence of the touring West Indies cricket side, who were not expected to be familiar with the individual players, was also cited. It wasn’t until June 1939, though, that the Football League took a vote to introduce squad numbers. It passed 24-20, and it was decided both teams should wear 1-11, but in strict order, as though the formation had been laid out on a page with the goalkeeper at the top.

This was complicated by the fact that, although almost every team by that stage had responded to the 1925 change in the offside law by adopting the W-M formation (a 3-2-2-3), there was still a belief that the “right” way to play was a 2-3-5. Thus the goalkeeper wore No 1, the right-back No 2, the left-back No 3, the right-half No 4, the centre-half No 5 and so on up to the centre-forward in No 9, the inside-left in No 10 and the left-winger in No 11. In practice, though, the centre-half (5), played between the full-backs (2 and 3) while the inside-forwards (8 and 10) played deeper than the wingers and centre-forward (7, 9 and 11).

Numbers rapidly became sacrosanct. When Hungary came to Wembley in 1953 and became the first foreign side to beat England at the national stadium, they provoked consternation because they were “incorrectly” numbered. The centre-back Mihaly Lantos wore No 4. The midfield creator Jozsef Bozsik wore No 5. Most bafflingly of all, Nandor Hidegkuti, the No 9, didn’t play as a centre-forward but created from midfield. What was Harry Johnston, England’s hapless centre-half, to do? Convention said he, the No 5, should pick up the No 9, but if he did that he left a huge hole in the back line. And if he did not, Hidegkuti was free to pick England apart.

The introspection provoked by that defeat led within a decade or so to a number of leading English teams adopting a back four, usually by withdrawing the left-half (the No 6) into the defensive line. As Alf Ramsey’s 1966 World Cup winners showed the value of packing midfield, so the wingers dropped back, leaving a 4-4-2 that lined up: 1; 2, 5, 6, 3; 7, 4, 8, 11; 9, 10. Within that, the No 4 would usually be the more defensive of the two central midfielders, while the No 10 retained some of the qualities of the inside-left, which is to say he tended to be the smaller, more creative forward alongside a big, physical number No 9.

Other countries, though, followed a different path. In Argentina, for instance, there had been no sudden shift to W-M in the late 1920s but, at River Plate in the late 1930s, the right-half Norberto Yácono, nicknamed “the Stamp” for his tight marking, would pick up the opposing creator. As other teams followed the principle, the number No 4 became a de facto third back, but operating on the right. No 4 remains the standard number for an Argentinian right-back, as exemplified by Javier Zanetti, for whom Inter retired the shirt. When Argentina switched to a back four after the humiliation of the 6-1 defeat to Czechoslovakia at the 1958 World Cup, the left-half fell into the back line, so a standard Argentinian back four would read: 4, 2, 6, 3. The No 5 remained as the caudillo in midfield, almost as venerated as the No 10 in the form of Antonio Rattín, Américo Gallego and Javier Mascherano.

In Brazil, though, there had been no widespread conversion of the right-half into a right-back, and so when the back four was adopted, the wing-halves simply dropped either side of the full-backs, leaving a standard back four as: 4, 2, 3, 6. The great right-back Carlos Alberto, for instance, wore No 4 at the 1970 World Cup, while the left-back Roberto Carlos tended to wear No 6. When, at Flamengo in the 1940s, Flávio Costa tipped the midfield square of Dori Kürschner’s W-M to create his diagonal, a major step towards 4-2-4, the No 5 became the more defensive central midfielder – leading to players such as Clodoaldo, Mauro Silva and Casemiro wearing the shirt for the national team – while the inside-left, the No 10, became the most creative midfielder.

In other countries, other conventions emerged. It was in the Netherlands and West Germany that the standard delineations of the expectations on midfielders in a 4-3-3 emerged. The No 6 would be the deep-lying player, the No 10 would be the creator, and the No 8 would be a box-to-box player shuttling between them. Or in France, where a five-man bench from which a manger could use two substitutes was adopted in 1976, it became standard for the reserve goalkeeper to wear No 16. Many goalkeepers in the Francophone world gained their first experience wearing No 16 and so favoured it when squad numbers were introduced: that’s why Fabian Barthez wore No 16 at the 1998 World Cup and Cameroon’s Thomas N’Kono wore it in 1990.

Numbers now are often a matter of personal choice and of brand-building. In a squad system, players can take on a familiar number and hope to embody its spirit, or try to make a more obscure number their own, as Johan Cruyff did with the No 14 more than half a century ago.

Numbers have a past, and they tell a story. Nobody on the Football League committee that narrowly voted to mandate squad numbers in 1939 would have considered the possibility, but in numbers are written the deep history of a country’s tactical development.

#871. Wales call up MK Dons' Collins as Moore withdraws

Aaron Collins (right) has seven goals in the past three games for MK Dons and is the EFL's joint-top goalscorer

Wales have called up uncapped MK Dons striker Aaron Collins for this month's Nations League matches following Wrexham frontman Kieffer Moore's withdrawal due to injury.

Moore, 34, left the field during Wrexham's 1-1 Championship draw with Wolves on Saturday.

Wales have not specified what kind of injury the 57-cap forward has sustained.

He is replaced in the Wales squad by Collins, who has scored 17 goals in 16 games across all competitions for League One side Dons this season, including four goals in a game against Doncaster last month.

The 29-year-old former Newport County player joins Craig Bellamy's squad for concluding Group A4 games in Norway and at home to Portugal.

Newport-born Collins has played for 10 different - mainly lower league - clubs since leaving Rodney Parade for Wolverhampton Wanderers in 2016.

Wales, who are looking to preserve their place in the Nations League's top tier, face Norway in Oslo on Saturday before finishing their campaign at home against Portugal next Tuesday.

Wales are third in Group A4, with their only win from four matches so far coming against World Cup quarter-finalists Norway in Cardiff last month.

Bellamy is without midfielder Jordan James but has influential Leeds pair Harry Wilson and Joe Rodon back, along with Cardiff playmaker Rubin Colwill.

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC Two Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live Sports Extra, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

Bellamy's side could still finish in second, third or fourth place.

A top-two spot would take Wales to the Nations League quarter-finals in March 2027.

Finishing third would mean a relegation play-off against a League B team in March, while finishing bottom of the group would result in either a relegation play-off or direct relegation, depending on the ranking with other League A groups.
